entries.heading: The ideas
entries.text: A neuron is a small calculator: output = activation(Σ input × weight + bias). A weight says how strongly one input matters; its sign says whether it pushes the total up or down. The bias shifts the total; the activation decides what leaves the neuron. A forward pass is the same calculation repeated layer by layer, left to right.

entries.heading: Student challenge
entries.text: In the original example, what changes if the bias goes from −1 to −5?

entries.heading: Reveal the worked answer
entries.text: Short answer: the output goes from 3 to 0 , and the neuron switches off.

entries.heading: What is the neuron doing?
entries.text: A neuron is a tiny calculator. Each input is multiplied by a weight (how strongly that input matters), the products are added, a bias is added (a starting offset), and an activation decides what leaves the neuron. Here the inputs are 2 and 3, the weights are 0.5 and 1, the bias is −1, and the activation is ReLU. 2 × 0.5 = 1 and 3 × 1 = 3 , so the total is 4 . With the original bias: 4 + (−1) = 3 . ReLU lets positive totals through, so the output is 3 . With bias −5: 4 + (−5) = −1 . ReLU blocks negative totals and returns 0 . The neuron is off: it sends no signal to the next layer.

entries.heading: What the numbers mean
entries.text: Input: a number the neuron receives. Here 2 and 3. Weight: a volume knob for one input. A bigger weight makes that input matter more. Bias: a starting offset added after the weighted sum. Negative makes the neuron harder to turn on. ReLU: a gate. Positive in, same number out. Negative in, zero out. Output: the signal this neuron sends forward. Target: the answer we want. Here the target is 1. Loss: a wrongness score, (output − target)² . Lower is better.

entries.heading: What if we try different biases?
entries.text: The weighted total before the bias is always 4. The bias shifts it, and ReLU cuts off anything below zero: Bias Total after bias Output Loss if target is 1 −10 −6 0 1 −5 −1 0 1 −3 1 1 0 −1 (original) 3 3 4 0 4 4 9 The turning point is between bias −4 and −3: at −4 the total is 0 and the output is 0; at −3 the total is 1 and the output is 1. Bias −1 leaves the neuron fully on at 3. Bias −5 is past the switch, so the neuron is fully off.

entries.heading: So is bias −5 “better”?
entries.text: For this one example it happens to give a lower loss: output 0 is wrong by 1, while output 3 is wrong by 2. But that is not a general rule. If the target were 3, bias −1 would give loss 0 and bias −5 would give loss 9. The target decides what a good output is; the bias only shifts the neuron.

entries.heading: What if we change something else?
entries.text: Change a weight: weights scale each input separately. Setting the first weight to 0 makes the total 3, so with bias −1 the output becomes 2. The bias then shifts that new total. Change the activation to linear: bias −5 would output −1 instead of 0. The next layer would receive a negative signal. ReLU's gate is what turns −1 into 0. Make every neuron in a layer negative: the whole layer outputs zeros. ReLU's slope is zero there, so the training signal is also zero; those neurons may stop learning. This is called a dead ReLU, and it is why biases and starting weights matter. The big idea: the bias is a threshold knob. It does not change the inputs; it changes how easily the neuron turns on. A small bias change can switch a neuron completely off and change every layer after it. In a language model, thousands of neurons like this work together, and their weights and biases are learned from text instead of typed by hand. The same questions still apply: what are the inputs, how strongly are they weighted, and does the activation let the result through? Try bias −5 Try bias −3 Back to original These buttons keep the current weights and only change the last bias. They run a forward pass; they do not train the network.

entries.heading: The ideas
entries.text: Training repeats four moves: forward pass, measure the loss, backpropagate, update the weights. The loss (mean squared error) is one number that says how wrong all the predictions are. The learning rate is the size of each correction: too large overshoots, too small crawls. One example can be memorised; a set of examples teaches a rule.

entries.heading: How training works
entries.text: Use labeled examples to teach the network what output to make. Forward pass Use the current weights and biases to make a prediction. Mean squared error Square each gap between the prediction and target, then take the average. Backpropagation Work backward to find how each weight and bias affects the loss. Gradient descent Subtract the learning rate times the gradient from each parameter, using all examples in one step. Load AND gate Four examples. The target is 1 only when both inputs are 1.

entries.heading: The ideas
entries.text: Backpropagation is the chain rule: multiply the slopes along the path from the loss back to a weight. δ (delta) is a neuron’s share of the error: the error arriving × the activation’s slope. A weight’s gradient is δ × the input that weight carried. A ReLU that is switched off has slope 0, so no error passes and nothing behind it learns.

entries.heading: The ideas
entries.text: One neuron can only draw a straight line; hidden layers combine lines into curves. Each hidden neuron learns its own small feature; the output mixes them. More neurons can fit harder patterns, but they can also memorise noise (overfitting). Training loss and test loss tell you whether the network learned the rule or the examples.

entries.heading: The ideas
entries.text: Data is split three ways: train to learn, validation to tune, test to judge once at the end. Features are scaled so that no input dominates only because its numbers are larger. A batch is a handful of examples per update; an epoch is one pass over all the training data. The test error, not the training error, is the honest measure of a model.

entries.heading: Define the task
entries.text: Define Decide what the network should learn.

entries.heading: Our goal
entries.text: Predict a house’s price from two things we know about it: its area and its number of bedrooms.

entries.heading: Inputs and target
entries.text: x₁ = area (m²), x₂ = bedrooms, and the target = the actual price in OMR. One house is one example; 1,000 houses are 1,000 examples.

entries.heading: Why the target is not an input
entries.text: The price is never fed into the network. It is only used after the prediction to measure the error. If we gave the network the answer, it would not learn to predict anything. Student check: In House 1, point to the two inputs (120, 2) and the target (45,000 OMR). Previous 1 / 10 Next step

entries.heading: Collect and clean the data
entries.text: Collect Gather real records, then fix the problems before training.

entries.heading: What a record contains
entries.text: Each record has two input features — area and bedrooms — and one target, the actual price. The target is used for comparison, not as an input.

entries.heading: What cleaning means
entries.text: Correct wrong units, fill or remove missing values, and remove accidental duplicate houses. A model trained on messy data learns the mess.

entries.heading: In our example
entries.text: 1,000 training houses plus separate validation and test houses. The first rows are 120 m² / 2 bedrooms / 45,000 OMR, 180 / 3 / 65,000, and 250 / 4 / 90,000. Student check: Which column is not an input? The price. It is the target. Previous 2 / 10 Next step

entries.heading: Split the data
entries.text: Split Keep some houses out of training so you can check whether the network really learned.

entries.heading: The three sets
entries.text: Training houses teach the weights and biases. Validation houses help compare settings and network designs without updating the weights. Test houses are opened once at the end to estimate performance on unseen houses.

entries.heading: In our example
entries.text: 1,000 training houses, 100 validation houses, and 100 test houses. The model never trains on the validation or test houses.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: A network can memorise the training houses. A separate set tells you whether it can handle a house it has never seen. Student check: Which set may update the weights? Only the training set. Previous 3 / 10 Next step

entries.heading: Prepare and scale the inputs
entries.text: Prepare Put the features on comparable scales so one large column does not dominate the learning.

entries.heading: The scales are different
entries.text: Area runs from about 80 to 300 m²; bedrooms run from 1 to 5. Without scaling, area would produce much larger products and gradients than bedrooms.

entries.heading: How scaling works
entries.text: For each feature, subtract the training mean and divide by the training standard deviation: x_scaled = (x − mean) / std. Fit the scaler on the training data only, then apply exactly the same numbers to validation and test houses.

entries.heading: The target
entries.text: The price is also scaled during training for stable gradients. The app converts every prediction back to OMR for the table and the error report. Student check: Why must the validation and test houses use the training mean and standard deviation? So the same transformation is applied to every house. Previous 4 / 10 Next step

entries.heading: Make the columns comparable
entries.text: x_scaled = (x − mean) / std Area 80–300 scaled Bedrooms 1–5 scaled Fit the mean and standard deviation on the training houses, then reuse them for validation and test houses.

entries.heading: Choose the network
entries.text: Choose Turn the problem into a shape: two inputs, a small hidden layer, one output.

entries.heading: The shape
entries.text: 2 input nodes (area and bedrooms) → 3 hidden neurons (ReLU) → 1 output neuron (Linear), because we predict one price. This gives 2×3 + 3×1 = 9 weights and 3 + 1 = 4 biases.

entries.heading: What each part does
entries.text: The hidden neurons learn combinations of area and bedrooms. The output neuron turns those features into a price. The output is linear because a price can be any positive number.

entries.heading: If the problem changes
entries.text: Add house age as a third feature and the input layer needs three nodes. Change the batch size from 100 to 50 and the input layer still needs two nodes, because each house still has two features. Input count follows features, not rows.

entries.heading: More hidden layers?
entries.text: A deeper 2 → 4 → 4 → 1 network has four neurons in each hidden layer. More capacity can learn more complex patterns, but it does not automatically improve results and can overfit. Compare designs on separate validation houses. Student check: Count the parameters: 9 weights and 4 biases. Where do the 9 weights come from? Previous 5 / 10 Next step

entries.text: Initialize Pick the learning settings, then set the starting weights reproducibly.

entries.heading: The settings
entries.text: Batch size 100, a learning rate, 10 epochs, mean squared error, and a small mini-batch optimizer. These are choices to test, not magic numbers.

entries.heading: The seed
entries.text: Seed 42 makes the random starting weights repeatable. Set seeds before other random operations too, such as splitting or shuffling the houses.

entries.heading: The starting point
entries.text: The two weight matrices start from a seeded random draw; the four biases start at zero. The same seed with the same initialization code gives the same starting network. entries.heading: Train using batches
entries.text: Batches The same network predicts 100 houses, averages their errors, and updates once.

entries.heading: One batch
entries.text: A batch of 100 houses has shape 100 × 2: 100 rows, and two feature columns per row. That is 200 input values. The network produces 100 price predictions.

entries.heading: One update
entries.text: The losses for those 100 predictions are averaged into one batch loss. Backpropagation calculates the gradients, and the optimizer updates every weight and bias once. The next batch uses the updated parameters.

entries.heading: Why batches?
entries.text: Computers process the rows together with matrix operations; you do not need 100 separate networks. Batches reduce memory needs and allow frequent updates. Student check: What is the shape of one batch? 100 examples × 2 features = 200 input values. Previous 7 / 10 Next step

entries.heading: One batch = 100 houses
entries.text: 100 examples × 2 features = 200 input values Predict 100 prices Average the losses Backpropagate Update once The same network predicts all 100 houses. You do not need 100 separate networks.

entries.heading: Repeat across epochs
entries.text: Epochs One pass over the training houses is one epoch. Keep the learned weights.

entries.heading: One epoch
entries.text: 1,000 training houses ÷ 100 per batch = 10 batches = 10 updates. After the 10th batch, every training house has been seen once.

entries.heading: The next epoch
entries.text: Shuffle the training houses and repeat. Do not reinitialize the weights: the second epoch starts from the parameters learned in the first.

entries.heading: Ten epochs
entries.text: 10 epochs × 10 batches = 100 updates. Each house is used once per epoch, then again in later epochs. The learned weights continue across epochs. Student check: After the first batch of epoch 2, how many updates have happened? 11. Previous 8 / 10 Next step

entries.heading: 10 batches = 1 epoch
entries.text: 1,000 training houses ÷ 100 batches 10 updates 1 epoch Shuffle and repeat. Keep the learned weights; do not initialize them again.

entries.heading: Validate and improve
entries.text: Validate Use the validation houses to choose settings, not to update the weights.

entries.heading: What we measure
entries.text: After each epoch, predict the validation houses and record the error. No gradient step is taken from validation data.

entries.heading: When to stop
entries.text: If validation performance stops improving, stop rather than assuming more training is always better. This is early stopping.

entries.heading: Capacity and overfitting
entries.text: More hidden layers can learn more complex patterns but may memorise the training houses. Compare a shallow 2 → 3 → 1 network with a deeper 2 → 4 → 4 → 1 network on the same validation split and choose by validation error, not by training error. entries.heading: Prepare and scale the inputs
entries.text: Scale Put study hours and attendance on comparable scales before training.

entries.heading: The scales are different
entries.text: Study hours run from about 1 to 20; attendance runs from 50 to 100. Without scaling, attendance would produce much larger products and gradients than study hours.

entries.heading: How scaling works
entries.text: For each feature, subtract the training mean and divide by the training standard deviation: x_scaled = (x − mean) / std. Fit the scaler on training students only, then apply the same numbers to validation and test students.

entries.heading: The target
entries.text: The score is also scaled while training for stable gradients. The app converts every prediction back to a score out of 100 for the tables and the error report. entries.heading: Choose the network
entries.text: Network The same small network as before: two inputs, three hidden neurons, one output.

entries.heading: The shape
entries.text: 2 input nodes (study hours and attendance) → 3 hidden neurons (ReLU) → 1 output neuron (Linear), because we predict one score. This gives 2×3 + 3×1 = 9 weights and 3 + 1 = 4 biases.

entries.heading: What each part does
entries.text: The hidden neurons learn combinations of study habits. The output neuron turns those features into a predicted score. The output is linear because a score can take any value in the 0–100 range.

entries.heading: Features are not rows
entries.text: Add a third feature, such as sleep hours, and the input layer needs three nodes. Change the batch size from 100 to 50 and the input layer still needs two nodes, because each student still has two features.

entries.heading: More hidden layers?
entries.text: A deeper 2 → 4 → 4 → 1 network has more capacity. More capacity can learn more complex patterns, but it does not automatically improve results and can overfit. entries.text: Batch The same network predicts 100 students, averages their errors, and updates once.

entries.heading: One batch
entries.text: A batch of 100 students has shape 100 × 2: 100 rows and two feature columns per row. That is 200 input values. The network produces 100 score predictions.

entries.heading: One update
entries.text: The losses for those 100 predictions are averaged into one batch loss. Backpropagation calculates the gradients, and the optimizer updates every weight and bias once. The next batch starts from those updated parameters.

entries.heading: Why batches?
entries.text: The rows are processed together with matrix operations; you do not need 100 separate networks. Batches reduce memory needs and allow frequent updates. Student check: What is the shape of one batch? 100 students × 2 features = 200 input values. Previous 7 / 10 Next step

entries.heading: The ideas behind the numbers
entries.text: House example: x₁ = area , x₂ = bedrooms , target = actual price , output = predicted price . The target is compared with the output; it is never an input feature.

entries.heading: Why do two input features not mean two training examples?
entries.text: A feature is a column: area and bedrooms. An example is a row: one house. One thousand houses are 1,000 examples with 2 features each, not 2 examples. The network receives 2 input values per row.

entries.heading: Why do 100 examples per batch not mean 100 weights?
entries.text: A weight connects two units in the network. In a 2 → 3 → 1 network there are 2×3 + 3×1 = 9 weights, regardless of batch size. Batch size is the number of rows processed together before one optimizer update.

entries.heading: Why is the same network reused for every batch?
entries.text: There is one set of weights and biases. Each batch uses the current parameters, computes a loss, and updates those same parameters. You do not create a new network for each batch.

entries.heading: Why do updated weights continue into the next batch and epoch?
entries.text: After each optimizer step, the new weights are the starting point for the next batch. After the last batch, the next epoch starts from those learned weights; the network is not reinitialized.

entries.heading: Why does adding hidden layers not automatically improve predictions?
entries.text: A hidden layer adds capacity, which can help with complex patterns. It can also overfit, add computation, and make optimization harder. More layers are a design choice to compare on validation data, not a guaranteed improvement.

entries.heading: Why should validation performance guide architecture comparisons?
entries.text: Training loss can keep falling while the network memorizes the training houses. Validation houses are not used for weight updates, so their loss tests whether the learned pattern generalizes. Choose the design by validation performance, then open the test set once. Worked example

entries.heading: The house-price network
entries.text: Use this setup Fully connected 2 → 3 → 1 with biases, 1,000 training houses, batch size 100, 20 epochs. Weights 9 2×3 + 3×1 Biases 4 3 + 1 Trainable 13 9 + 4 Batches / epoch 10 1,000 ÷ 100 Updates / epoch 10 one per batch 20 epochs 200 updates float32 storage 52 B 13 × 4 bytes CPU Appropriate GPU unnecessary All 100 houses in a batch use the same current parameters. The network predicts 100 prices, their losses are averaged, gradients are calculated, and the optimizer updates the 13 parameters once. The next batch starts from those updated parameters. Parameter storage is 52 bytes; total training memory is larger because of gradients, optimizer state, activations, data, and framework overhead. The tiny size is exactly why a CPU is a good fit. 15-second check: 9 weights + 4 biases = 13 parameters; 1,000 ÷ 100 = 10 batches; 10 × 20 = 200 updates.

entries.heading: 01Set up the environmentCreate an isolated Python environment and install the libraries the guide uses.
entries.title: 01 Set up the environment Create an isolated Python environment and install the libraries the guide uses.
entries.text: Purpose Create an isolated Python environment and install the libraries the guide uses. Input A terminal and Python 3.10+; the selected execution device. What the code does The terminal commands create a virtual environment so this project does not affect other Python work. Activate it before running any Python. Windows and macOS/Linux use different activation commands. Keep terminal commands out of the Python file. Terminal commands (not Python) Copy code # Windows PowerShell py -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 # If PowerShell blocks the activation script, allow it for this terminal only: # Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install torch pandas numpy scikit-learn matplotlib python -m pip install notebook # macOS / Linux python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install torch pandas numpy scikit-learn matplotlib python -m pip install notebook # GPU users: install PyTorch with the official selector instead of guessing CUDA commands: # https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/ # Choose your OS, package manager, and CUDA version there. This guide never guesses a CUDA wheel. Step 1 Python code Copy code import sys print("Python:", sys.version.split()[0]) try: import torch import pandas import numpy import sklearn import matplotlib except ImportError as error: raise SystemExit( f"Missing package: {error}. Run the installation commands from Step 1 in your own terminal." ) from error print("torch:", torch.__version__) print("pandas:", pandas.__version__) print("numpy:", numpy.__version__) print("scikit-learn:", sklearn.__version__) print("CUDA available:", torch.cuda.is_available()) Output Python and package versions, plus whether CUDA is available. Check before continuing All imports succeed and CUDA available is False (CPU is the intended default).

entries.heading: 02Import libraries and set seedsImport every library once and make random choices repeatable before data generation, splitting, and initialization.
entries.title: 02 Import libraries and set seeds Import every library once and make random choices repeatable before data generation, splitting, and initialization.
entries.text: Purpose Import every library once and make random choices repeatable before data generation, splitting, and initialization. Input The virtual environment from Step 1 and the selected seed. What the code does The seed controls random choices such as synthetic rows, the split order, and the initial weights. It does not determine how many weights exist. It is set once before the workflow; resetting it inside the loop would restart the randomness. Exact bit-for-bit reproducibility can still vary across hardware, library versions, and nondeterministic operations. Step 2 Python code Copy code # === Step 2: imports and reproducible seeds === import copy import math import random from pathlib import Path import matplotlib matplotlib.use("Agg") # headless-safe; remove this line if you want interactive plot windows import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd import torch from torch import nn from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler SEED = 42 random.seed(SEED) np.random.seed(SEED) torch.manual_seed(SEED) if torch.cuda.is_available(): torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(SEED) torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False print("Seed:", SEED) # Do not reset these seeds inside a batch or epoch loop: the seed starts the run; # it does not set the number of weights or make every hardware stack bit-identical. Output Seed value 42; imports are ready. Check before continuing The seed prints once. Do not add seed resets inside the batch or epoch loop.

entries.heading: 03Load and inspect the datasetLoad the selected data source, verify its columns, and understand what each row represents.
entries.title: 03 Load and inspect the dataset Load the selected data source, verify its columns, and understand what each row represents.
entries.text: Purpose Load the selected data source, verify its columns, and understand what each row represents. Input synthetic generic demonstration with 2 feature(s) and 1 target(s). What the code does This guide has no external real dataset, so it generates an explicitly labeled generic demonstration dataset from your seed. These are synthetic classroom records, not real observations. You can replace the data-loading block with your CSV later and keep the rest of the workflow. Step 3 Python code Copy code # === Step 3: load and inspect the dataset === # Dataset configuration chosen in the guide. FEATURES = ["feature_1", "feature_2"] TARGETS = ["target_1"] SOURCE = "synthetic-generic" TRAIN_ROWS = 1000 VALIDATION_ROWS = 100 TEST_ROWS = 100 TOTAL_ROWS = TRAIN_ROWS + VALIDATION_ROWS + TEST_ROWS BATCH_SIZE = 100 EPOCHS = 20 LEARNING_RATE = 1 OPTIMIZER_NAME = "sgd" DEVICE_NAME = "cpu" TARGET_SCALED = True EARLY_STOPPING = False PATIENCE = 5 NEW_EXAMPLE_VALUES = [0, 1] print("Dataset source:", SOURCE) def make_generic_data(seed, n_rows): """Synthetic classroom data only; these are not real observations.""" rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) features = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, size=(n_rows, len(FEATURES))) coefficients = np.linspace(3.0, 0.5, len(FEATURES)) base = features @ coefficients + 2.0 if len(TARGETS) == 1: target = (base + rng.normal(0.0, 0.4, size=n_rows)).reshape(-1, 1) return pd.DataFrame(np.column_stack([features, target]), columns=FEATURES + TARGETS) targets = np.column_stack([ base + index * 0.5 + rng.normal(0.0, 0.4, size=n_rows) for index in range(len(TARGETS)) ]) return pd.DataFrame(np.column_stack([features, targets]), columns=FEATURES + TARGETS) df = make_generic_data(SEED, TOTAL_ROWS) print("Rows:", len(df)) print("Columns:", list(df.columns)) print("Data types:") print(df.dtypes) print("First rows:") print(df.head()) print("Missing values by column:") print(df.isna().sum()) print("Features:", FEATURES) print("Targets:", TARGETS) assert len(df) == TOTAL_ROWS, f"Expected {TOTAL_ROWS} rows, found {len(df)}." assert list(df.columns) == FEATURES + TARGETS print("Total dataset rows:", TOTAL_ROWS) print("Training rows:", TRAIN_ROWS, "| validation:", VALIDATION_ROWS, "| test:", TEST_ROWS) Output 1200 rows; column names and types; the first rows; missing-value counts; feature and target lists. Check before continuing The row count matches the split total, both feature columns and the target are numeric, and you see the expected column names and a few sensible rows. Remember: synthetic does not mean real.

entries.heading: 04Clean and split the dataValidate columns, handle invalid values, and create training, validation, and test sets without leaking information.
entries.title: 04 Clean and split the data Validate columns, handle invalid values, and create training, validation, and test sets without leaking information.
entries.text: Purpose Validate columns, handle invalid values, and create training, validation, and test sets without leaking information. Input The inspected DataFrame, seed 42, and split counts 1000/100/100. What the code does The code coerces values to numeric, drops rows with missing targets, and splits before fitting preprocessing. The imputer is fit on the training partition only, then applied to validation and test. The total dataset is larger than the training set; only the training rows update weights. Step 4 Python code Copy code # === Step 4: clean and split the data === REQUIRED_COLUMNS = FEATURES + TARGETS missing_columns = [column for column in REQUIRED_COLUMNS if column not in df.columns] assert not missing_columns, f"Missing required columns: {missing_columns}" clean_df = df[REQUIRED_COLUMNS].copy() for column in REQUIRED_COLUMNS: clean_df[column] = pd.to_numeric(clean_df[column], errors="coerce") # A missing target cannot be used as a supervised label; drop it before splitting. clean_df = clean_df.dropna(subset=TARGETS).reset_index(drop=True) assert len(clean_df) == TOTAL_ROWS, ( f"Cleaning changed the expected row count: {len(clean_df)} instead of {TOTAL_ROWS}. " "Check missing targets or invalid numeric values." ) # Split first, then fit imputation on the training partition only. split_rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED) order = split_rng.permutation(len(clean_df)) train_df = clean_df.iloc[order[:TRAIN_ROWS]].copy() validation_df = clean_df.iloc[order[TRAIN_ROWS:TRAIN_ROWS + VALIDATION_ROWS]].copy() test_df = clean_df.iloc[order[TRAIN_ROWS + VALIDATION_ROWS:]].copy() feature_imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="median") X_train = feature_imputer.fit_transform(train_df[FEATURES]) X_validation = feature_imputer.transform(validation_df[FEATURES]) X_test = feature_imputer.transform(test_df[FEATURES]) y_train = train_df[TARGETS].to_numpy(dtype=float) y_validation = validation_df[TARGETS].to_numpy(dtype=float) y_test = test_df[TARGETS].to_numpy(dtype=float) print("Train examples:", len(train_df)) print("Validation examples:", len(validation_df)) print("Test examples:", len(test_df)) print("Total examples:", len(clean_df), "— only", len(train_df), "are used for weight updates.") print("Training feature matrix:", X_train.shape, "| train targets:", y_train.shape) assert len(train_df) + len(validation_df) + len(test_df) == TOTAL_ROWS # The imputer was fit on training data only; validation/test use that fitted imputer. Output Training: 1000; validation: 100; test: 100; total: 1200. Check before continuing The three split sizes sum to the total. Validation and test were held out. No imputer statistic was learned from them.

entries.heading: 05Scale featuresPut features on comparable scales and optionally standardize the target for optimization.
entries.title: 05 Scale features Put features on comparable scales and optionally standardize the target for optimization.
entries.text: Purpose Put features on comparable scales and optionally standardize the target for optimization. Input Training, validation, and test arrays from Step 4. What the code does Scaling helps gradient-based training when features have different units, such as square metres and bedroom counts. The scaler is fit on training only. If target scaling is used, the target scaler must be kept so predictions can be converted back to prices. Step 5 Python code Copy code # === Step 5: scale features (and optionally the target) === feature_scaler = StandardScaler() X_train_scaled = feature_scaler.fit_transform(X_train) X_validation_scaled = feature_scaler.transform(X_validation) X_test_scaled = feature_scaler.transform(X_test) if TARGET_SCALED: target_scaler = StandardScaler() y_train_scaled = target_scaler.fit_transform(y_train) y_validation_scaled = target_scaler.transform(y_validation) y_test_scaled = target_scaler.transform(y_test) else: target_scaler = None y_train_scaled = y_train y_validation_scaled = y_validation y_test_scaled = y_test print("Feature means (training):", np.round(feature_scaler.mean_, 3)) print("Feature scales (training):", np.round(feature_scaler.scale_, 3)) print("Target scaled:", TARGET_SCALED) print("Scaled training features:", X_train_scaled.shape) # Fit on training only. Reusing the training scaler is what keeps validation/test comparable. Output Scaled feature shapes; training feature means and scales; whether the target is scaled. Check before continuing The scaler means and scales look plausible. Validation/test were transformed, not re-fit.

entries.heading: 06Create tensors and batchesConvert arrays to correctly shaped float32 tensors and create shuffled mini-batches.
entries.title: 06 Create tensors and batches Convert arrays to correctly shaped float32 tensors and create shuffled mini-batches.
entries.text: Purpose Convert arrays to correctly shaped float32 tensors and create shuffled mini-batches. Input Scaled arrays and batch size. What the code does The feature tensor is [1000, 2], and the target tensor is [1000, 1]. Rows are examples; columns are features. Batch size counts rows, not neurons or weights. The final batch may be smaller because drop_last=False. Training batches are shuffled each epoch. Step 6 Python code Copy code # === Step 6: tensors and mini-batches === X_train_tensor = torch.tensor(X_train_scaled, dtype=torch.float32) y_train_tensor = torch.tensor(y_train_scaled, dtype=torch.float32) X_validation_tensor = torch.tensor(X_validation_scaled, dtype=torch.float32) y_validation_tensor = torch.tensor(y_validation_scaled, dtype=torch.float32) X_test_tensor = torch.tensor(X_test_scaled, dtype=torch.float32) y_test_tensor = torch.tensor(y_test_scaled, dtype=torch.float32) train_dataset = TensorDataset(X_train_tensor, y_train_tensor) train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True, drop_last=False) validation_loader = DataLoader( TensorDataset(X_validation_tensor, y_validation_tensor), batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=False, drop_last=False, ) test_loader = DataLoader( TensorDataset(X_test_tensor, y_test_tensor), batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=False, drop_last=False, ) batch_sizes = [batch.shape[0] for batch, _ in train_loader] print("Training feature tensor:", tuple(X_train_tensor.shape), "= [examples, features]") print("Training target tensor:", tuple(y_train_tensor.shape), "= [examples, targets]") print("Training examples:", len(train_dataset)) print("Batch size:", BATCH_SIZE) print("Batches per epoch:", len(train_loader)) print("Batch sizes:", batch_sizes[:5], "..." if len(batch_sizes) > 5 else "", "last:", batch_sizes[-1] if batch_sizes else 0) assert len(train_loader) == math.ceil(TRAIN_ROWS / BATCH_SIZE) # drop_last=False retains the final smaller batch. One optimizer update happens per batch. Output 1000 training examples, 10 batch(es) per epoch, and the first/last batch sizes. Check before continuing The tensor shapes and batch count match the training split. A final batch may be smaller; it is retained.

entries.heading: 07Build and inspect the networkBuild exactly the selected fully connected architecture, activation functions, and output layer.
entries.title: 07 Build and inspect the network Build exactly the selected fully connected architecture, activation functions, and output layer.
entries.text: Purpose Build exactly the selected fully connected architecture, activation functions, and output layer. Input The selected layer sizes/activations and the seed. What the code does The model is an nn.Sequential of Linear layers and the selected activations. The output activation stays exactly as selected. Initialization follows the lab family — uniform He for ReLU, Xavier otherwise, and zero biases — but cross-framework random streams are not identical. The code prints parameter shapes and the exact trainable count. Step 7 Python code Copy code # === Step 7: build and inspect the exact network === # Exact selected layers: # Layer 1: nn.Linear(2, 1) + relu MODEL_SPEC = [ { "in": 2, "out": 1, "activation": "relu" } ] EXPECTED_TRAINABLE = 3 OUTPUT_ACTIVATION = "relu" # NOTE: your selected output activation is relu. It can clip negative predictions; # ordinary house-price regression normally uses a linear output. This code keeps your selection. def activation_module(name): if name == "linear": return nn.Identity() if name == "relu": return nn.ReLU() if name == "sigmoid": return nn.Sigmoid() if name == "tanh": return nn.Tanh() raise ValueError(f"Unsupported activation: {name}") def build_model_from_spec(spec): modules = [] for layer in spec: modules.append(nn.Linear(layer["in"], layer["out"])) modules.append(activation_module(layer["activation"])) return nn.Sequential(*modules) def initialize_like_lab(model, spec): # Same initialization family as the lab: uniform He for ReLU, Xavier otherwise, # and explicitly zero biases. Cross-framework RNG streams are not identical. linear_layers = [module for module in model if isinstance(module, nn.Linear)] for layer, linear in zip(spec, linear_layers): fan_in = linear.weight.shape[1] fan_out = linear.weight.shape[0] limit = math.sqrt(6.0 / fan_in) if layer["activation"] == "relu" else math.sqrt(6.0 / (fan_in + fan_out)) nn.init.uniform_(linear.weight, -limit, limit) nn.init.zeros_(linear.bias) if DEVICE_NAME == "cuda" and not torch.cuda.is_available(): print("CUDA was requested but is not available; falling back to CPU.") device = torch.device("cpu") else: device = torch.device(DEVICE_NAME) torch.manual_seed(SEED) model = build_model_from_spec(MODEL_SPEC) initialize_like_lab(model, MODEL_SPEC) model = model.to(device) print(model) for name, parameter in model.named_parameters(): print(name, tuple(parameter.shape)) total_trainable = sum(parameter.numel() for parameter in model.parameters() if parameter.requires_grad) print("Total trainable parameters:", total_trainable) assert total_trainable == EXPECTED_TRAINABLE print("Output activation:", OUTPUT_ACTIVATION) print("Device:", device) # Biases are explicitly initialized to zero above. The seed controls initialization, # not the parameter count. Output Model structure; each parameter shape; total trainable parameters = 3 (2 weights + 1 biases). Check before continuing The parameter count is 3. For a 2 → 3 → 1 network with biases: 9 weights, 4 biases, 13 trainable parameters.

entries.heading: 08Define loss and optimizerCreate the selected optimizer and a loss suitable for regression.
entries.title: 08 Define loss and optimizer Create the selected optimizer and a loss suitable for regression.
entries.text: Purpose Create the selected optimizer and a loss suitable for regression. Input The model from Step 7, selected optimizer, and learning rate. What the code does MSE is used for this teaching regression example. MSE is in squared scaled target units; MAE (Step 13) is easier to read in original units such as OMR. Loss measures error, backpropagation computes gradients, and the optimizer applies one update per batch. Step 8 Python code Copy code # === Step 8: define the loss and optimizer === criterion = nn.MSELoss() if OPTIMIZER_NAME == "adam": optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE) else: optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE) print("Loss:", criterion) print("Optimizer:", optimizer) # Loss measures prediction error. Backpropagation computes gradients. # The optimizer turns those gradients into one parameter update per batch. Output Loss object MSE (scaled target) and the SGD optimizer. Check before continuing MSE and the selected optimizer are shown. Do not confuse the loss with an accuracy score.

entries.heading: 09Inspect one training batchSee the actual forward pass, loss, gradients, and one optimizer step without changing the main experiment.
entries.title: 09 Inspect one training batch See the actual forward pass, loss, gradients, and one optimizer step without changing the main experiment.
entries.text: Purpose See the actual forward pass, loss, gradients, and one optimizer step without changing the main experiment. Input A copy of the model, an independent optimizer, and the first training batch. What the code does This optional demonstration uses copy.deepcopy(model) and a separate optimizer. It prints a limited subset, performs one step on the copy, and asserts that the main model is unchanged. The real training run below starts from the original model and optimizer. Step 9 Python code Copy code # === Step 9: optional inspection of one batch (does not touch the main run) === # A deep copy and a separate optimizer keep the experiment's model/optimizer state untouched. probe_model = copy.deepcopy(model) if OPTIMIZER_NAME == "adam": probe_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(probe_model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE) else: probe_optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(probe_model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE) probe_model.train() probe_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=False, drop_last=False) X_probe, y_probe = next(iter(probe_loader)) X_probe = X_probe.to(device) y_probe = y_probe.to(device) initial_main_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()) before = [parameter.detach().clone() for parameter in probe_model.parameters()] probe_optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) predictions = probe_model(X_probe) loss = criterion(predictions, y_probe) loss.backward() print("Parameter before the step (first 5 values):", before[0].flatten()[:5].cpu()) print("Predictions (scaled target units, first 5):", predictions[:5].detach().cpu().flatten()) print("Targets (scaled target units, first 5):", y_probe[:5].cpu().flatten()) print("Batch loss:", loss.item()) print("Gradient of the first weight (first 5 values):", probe_model[0].weight.grad.flatten()[:5].cpu()) probe_optimizer.step() print("Parameter after one optimizer step (first 5 values):", next(probe_model.parameters()).detach().flatten()[:5].cpu()) main_unchanged = all( torch.equal(model.state_dict()[key], initial_main_state[key]) for key in initial_main_state ) print("Main model unchanged by the demonstration:", main_unchanged) assert main_unchanged # This demonstration is a copy. The main training run below still starts from the original model. Output A few parameter values, predictions, targets, batch loss, gradients, post-step values, and "Main model unchanged by the demonstration: True". Check before continuing The main model unchanged line is True. The printed arrays are labeled subsets, not full parameter dumps.

entries.heading: 10Run the complete training loopTrain the selected network for the selected epochs and track validation loss.
entries.title: 10 Run the complete training loop Train the selected network for the selected epochs and track validation loss.
entries.text: Purpose Train the selected network for the selected epochs and track validation loss. Input Model, optimizer, criterion, loaders, epochs, and early-stopping settings. What the code does Every batch follows the same six operations: move to device, clear gradients, forward, loss, backward, optimizer step. The next batch starts from the updated parameters. Epoch train loss is a sample-weighted average so a smaller final batch is handled correctly. Validation uses no_grad and no updates. The test set is not touched. Step 10 Python code Copy code # === Step 10: complete mini-batch training loop === def evaluate(current_model, loader, current_criterion, current_device): current_model.eval() total_loss = 0.0 total_examples = 0 with torch.no_grad(): for X_batch, y_batch in loader: X_batch = X_batch.to(current_device) y_batch = y_batch.to(current_device) predictions = current_model(X_batch) loss = current_criterion(predictions, y_batch) batch_examples = X_batch.shape[0] total_loss += loss.item() * batch_examples total_examples += batch_examples return total_loss / total_examples if total_examples else float("nan") history = {"train": [], "validation": []} best_validation_loss = float("inf") best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()) best_epoch = 0 epochs_without_improvement = 0 for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1): model.train() running_loss = 0.0 seen_examples = 0 for batch_index, (X_batch, y_batch) in enumerate(train_loader, start=1): # 1. Move the batch to the selected execution device. X_batch = X_batch.to(device) y_batch = y_batch.to(device) # 2. Clear the gradients from the previous batch. optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) # 3. Forward pass: current parameters produce predictions. predictions = model(X_batch) # 4. Calculate the batch loss. loss = criterion(predictions, y_batch) # 5. Backpropagation: calculate gradients. loss.backward() # 6. One optimizer step: update weights and biases. optimizer.step() batch_examples = X_batch.shape[0] running_loss += loss.item() * batch_examples seen_examples += batch_examples if batch_index == 1 or batch_index % 5 == 0 or batch_index == len(train_loader): print( f"Epoch {epoch:02d} | batch {batch_index:03d}/{len(train_loader):03d} " f"| batch loss {loss.item():.6f} | examples {batch_examples}" ) train_loss = running_loss / seen_examples validation_loss = evaluate(model, validation_loader, criterion, device) history["train"].append(train_loss) history["validation"].append(validation_loss) if validation_loss < best_validation_loss: best_validation_loss = validation_loss best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()) best_epoch = epoch epochs_without_improvement = 0 else: epochs_without_improvement += 1 print( f"Epoch {epoch:02d} summary | train loss {train_loss:.6f} " f"| validation loss {validation_loss:.6f} | best epoch {best_epoch}" ) if EARLY_STOPPING and epochs_without_improvement >= PATIENCE: print(f"Early stopping at epoch {epoch}: validation did not improve for {PATIENCE} epoch(s).") break print("Epochs completed:", len(history["train"])) print("Best epoch:", best_epoch, "| best validation loss:", best_validation_loss) # The next batch uses the parameters updated by the previous batch. # Parameters are not reset between batches or epochs. The test set was never touched here. Output 200 expected optimizer update(s): 10 batch(es) × 20 epoch(s). Batch logs are limited; each epoch prints a concise summary. Check before continuing Update counts match batches × epochs. Training and validation losses are recorded. No test data appears here.

entries.heading: 11Validate and select the modelExplain validation, preserve the best validation state, and restore it before final testing.
entries.title: 11 Validate and select the model Explain validation, preserve the best validation state, and restore it before final testing.
entries.text: Purpose Explain validation, preserve the best validation state, and restore it before final testing. Input The best validation state and validation loader from Step 10. What the code does The loop saved an independent copy of the state with the best validation loss. This step restores that state and reports the selected validation loss. Early stopping, when enabled, uses the selected patience and stops after that many epochs without improvement. The test set is never used for these decisions. Step 11 Python code Copy code # === Step 11: validate and restore the selected model === # Validation ran each epoch without gradients or parameter updates. # The test set was not used to choose the architecture or the stopping point. model.load_state_dict(best_state) model.eval() selected_validation_loss = evaluate(model, validation_loader, criterion, device) print("Selected epoch:", best_epoch) print("Selected validation loss:", selected_validation_loss) print("The test set has not been used for selection.") if EARLY_STOPPING: print(f"Early stopping was enabled with patience={PATIENCE}.") else: print("Early stopping was disabled; the best validation state is still restored.") Output Selected epoch, selected validation loss, and whether early stopping was enabled. Check before continuing The selected model is the best-validation checkpoint, not simply the last epoch. Test data is still untouched.

entries.heading: 12Plot learning progressCompare training and validation loss across epochs and look for overfitting.
entries.title: 12 Plot learning progress Compare training and validation loss across epochs and look for overfitting.
entries.text: Purpose Compare training and validation loss across epochs and look for overfitting. Input The history recorded during training. What the code does Falling loss means improving fit to that dataset. Training loss improving while validation loss worsens can indicate overfitting. More epochs or hidden layers do not guarantee better generalization; compare with validation evidence. Step 12 Python code Copy code # === Step 12: plot learning progress === epochs_ran = list(range(1, len(history["train"]) + 1)) plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5)) plt.plot(epochs_ran, history["train"], marker="o", label="Training loss") plt.plot(epochs_ran, history["validation"], marker="s", label="Validation loss") plt.title("Training and validation loss") plt.xlabel("Epoch") plt.ylabel("MSE (scaled target units)") plt.legend() plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3) plt.tight_layout() plt.savefig("learning_curves.png", dpi=150) if matplotlib.get_backend().lower() != "agg": plt.show() print("Saved learning_curves.png") # Falling loss means improving fit. Training improving while validation worsens can signal overfitting. # More epochs or hidden layers do not guarantee better generalization. Output A training/validation loss chart saved as learning_curves.png. Check before continuing The two curves use the same epoch axis. Look for a widening gap, not just a lower training loss.

entries.heading: 13Test the selected modelEvaluate the restored model once on the held-out test set and translate metrics into original units.
entries.title: 13 Test the selected model Evaluate the restored model once on the held-out test set and translate metrics into original units.
entries.text: Purpose Evaluate the restored model once on the held-out test set and translate metrics into original units. Input The selected model, test loader, and target scaler. What the code does The test set is used only now. MAE and RMSE are reported in original target units after inverting the target scaler. MSE is also reported in scaled target units. The table shows a small labeled subset of actual and predicted values. Step 13 Python code Copy code # === Step 13: test the selected model once === test_loss_scaled = evaluate(model, test_loader, criterion, device) model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): test_predictions_scaled = model(X_test_tensor.to(device)).cpu().numpy() if target_scaler is not None: test_predictions = target_scaler.inverse_transform(test_predictions_scaled) else: test_predictions = test_predictions_scaled test_actual = y_test mae = float(np.mean(np.abs(test_predictions - test_actual))) rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((test_predictions - test_actual) ** 2))) print("Test MSE (scaled target units):", test_loss_scaled) print("Test MAE (original target units):", mae) print("Test RMSE (original target units):", rmse) results = pd.DataFrame( np.column_stack([test_actual, test_predictions]), columns=[f"actual_{name}" for name in TARGETS] + [f"predicted_{name}" for name in TARGETS], ) print("Actual vs predicted (first 10 test rows):") print(results.head(10).to_string(index=False)) # Report these once. The test set is for the final check, not for tuning. Output Test MSE, MAE, RMSE, and the first 10 actual/predicted rows. Check before continuing Metrics are in understandable target units. Do not go back and tune on this test result; if you must, use a fresh test set.

entries.heading: 14Predict for a new exampleApply the saved training preprocessing and the selected model to one new set of feature values.
entries.title: 14 Predict for a new example Apply the saved training preprocessing and the selected model to one new set of feature values.
entries.text: Purpose Apply the saved training preprocessing and the selected model to one new set of feature values. Input A new example in feature order: feature_1, feature_2. What the code does The new row is imputed and scaled with the training artifacts, converted to a tensor, and passed through the model with no_grad. The target scaler is inverted so the answer is in original units. Inference does not update any weights. Step 14 Python code Copy code # === Step 14: predict a new example === if len(NEW_EXAMPLE_VALUES) != len(FEATURES): raise ValueError("The new example must contain one value per input feature.") new_example = dict(zip(FEATURES, NEW_EXAMPLE_VALUES)) new_frame = pd.DataFrame([new_example], columns=FEATURES) new_imputed = feature_imputer.transform(new_frame) new_scaled = feature_scaler.transform(new_imputed) new_tensor = torch.tensor(new_scaled, dtype=torch.float32).to(device) model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): new_prediction_scaled = model(new_tensor).cpu().numpy() if target_scaler is not None: new_prediction = target_scaler.inverse_transform(new_prediction_scaled) else: new_prediction = new_prediction_scaled print("New example (original feature order):", new_example) print("Predicted target (original units):", new_prediction.ravel()) # Inference uses the learned parameters without updating them. Output The new feature dictionary and the predicted target in original units. Check before continuing The feature values are in the original feature order. The prediction is a number, and no optimizer step occurred.

entries.heading: 15Save and reloadSave an inference-ready artifact and prove that reloading reproduces the prediction.
entries.title: 15 Save and reload Save an inference-ready artifact and prove that reloading reproduces the prediction.
entries.text: Purpose Save an inference-ready artifact and prove that reloading reproduces the prediction. Input The selected model, architecture, feature order, preprocessing, and configuration. What the code does The checkpoint stores weights, layer specs, activations, feature names, imputer, scalers, and the training configuration. Reloading builds the architecture from the saved specs, loads the weights, and compares before/after predictions. This is inference-only; resuming interrupted training also needs optimizer state, epoch, history, and RNG state. Step 15 Python code Copy code # === Step 15: save and reload for inference === CHECKPOINT_PATH = Path("trained_network_model.pt") checkpoint = { "state_dict": model.state_dict(), "layer_specs": MODEL_SPEC, "feature_names": FEATURES, "target_names": TARGETS, "feature_imputer": feature_imputer, "feature_scaler": feature_scaler, "target_scaler": target_scaler, "config": { "architecture": [layer["in"] for layer in MODEL_SPEC] + [MODEL_SPEC[-1]["out"]], "activations": [layer["activation"] for layer in MODEL_SPEC], "features": FEATURES, "targets": TARGETS, "train_rows": TRAIN_ROWS, "validation_rows": VALIDATION_ROWS, "test_rows": TEST_ROWS, "batch_size": BATCH_SIZE, "epochs": EPOCHS, "learning_rate": LEARNING_RATE, "optimizer": OPTIMIZER_NAME, "target_scaled": TARGET_SCALED, "seed": SEED, }, } torch.save(checkpoint, CHECKPOINT_PATH) print("Saved inference checkpoint:", CHECKPOINT_PATH) def predict_with_artifact(artifact, feature_values): frame = pd.DataFrame([dict(zip(artifact["feature_names"], feature_values))], columns=artifact["feature_names"]) features = artifact["feature_imputer"].transform(frame) features = artifact["feature_scaler"].transform(features) tensor = torch.tensor(features, dtype=torch.float32).to(device) loaded = build_model_from_spec(artifact["layer_specs"]) loaded.load_state_dict(artifact["state_dict"]) loaded.to(device) loaded.eval() with torch.no_grad(): prediction = loaded(tensor).cpu().numpy() if artifact["target_scaler"] is not None: prediction = artifact["target_scaler"].inverse_transform(prediction) return prediction before_reload = predict_with_artifact(checkpoint, NEW_EXAMPLE_VALUES) loaded_checkpoint = torch.load(CHECKPOINT_PATH, map_location=device, weights_only=False) loaded_model = build_model_from_spec(loaded_checkpoint["layer_specs"]) loaded_model.load_state_dict(loaded_checkpoint["state_dict"]) loaded_model.to(device) loaded_model.eval() after_reload = predict_with_artifact(loaded_checkpoint, NEW_EXAMPLE_VALUES) print("Prediction before reload:", before_reload.ravel()) print("Prediction after reload:", after_reload.ravel()) reload_matches = bool(np.allclose(before_reload, after_reload, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5)) print("Reloaded prediction matches:", reload_matches) assert reload_matches # This is an inference-only save: architecture, weights, feature order, imputer, scalers, and config. # To resume interrupted training, also save optimizer.state_dict(), the current epoch, history, # and the RNG state; inference does not need those. Output Saved trained_network_model.pt, predictions before and after reload, and "Reloaded prediction matches: True". Check before continuing The reloaded prediction matches. Keep the artifact and the feature order together; a model without its preprocessing is incomplete.

entries.heading: The ideas
entries.text: A model reads tokens, not letters or words: a token can be a whole word, part of a word, or punctuation. Every token has a fixed ID number; the model only ever sees these numbers. Token count and word count differ: Arabic, rare words, and emoji often need more tokens per word. Spaces count too: the space before a word usually belongs to that word’s token.

entries.heading: The big picture: every token has one fixed row
entries.text: 1 Your sentence The ship reached the port . 2 Tokenizer The ·ship ·reached ·the ·port . The → Token ID 976 3 Embedding table Token ID Stored vector 975 [ −0.33, −0.32, −0.31 , …] 976 [ +0.11, −0.65, +0.09 , …] 977 [ +0.08, −0.76, −0.40 , …] Look up row 976 4 Starting vector for The [ +0.11, −0.65, +0.09, −0.38, −0.03, −0.54, −1.16, +0.09 ] Key idea: the token ID selects the row, and the row supplies the vector. Real tokens and IDs from o200k_base; the vector numbers come from the demonstration table. Each token, not each word: a word can be split into several tokens, and each of them gets its own row. Your text, followed down to the table The The 976 ship ·ship 12407 reached ·reached 15237 the ·the 290 port ·port 3135 (symbol) . 13 Every word here is a single token. Longer or rarer words split: “photosynthesis” becomes ·photos (8309) + ynthesis (73972), two tokens and two rows. Inside the embedding table The table never changes while the model reads. It has 200,019 rows, one per ID, sorted by ID. Your text simply reads the rows it needs. A token that appears twice reads the same row twice. ID d1 … d 8 Used by ⋮ 13 other rows 13 . # 6 ⋮ 276 other rows 290 ·the # 4 ⋮ 685 other rows 976 The # 1 ⋮ 2,158 other rows 3,135 ·port # 5 ⋮ 9,271 other rows 12,407 ·ship # 2 ⋮ 2,829 other rows 15,237 ·reached # 3 ⋮ … up to row 200,018 When is each part fixed? Before training: the ID The tokenizer’s vocabulary is built first. Each piece of text gets its ID, and the ID never changes. The 976 During training: the numbers Row 976 starts as random numbers. Training nudges them a little after every example, so they become useful. The ID stays the same the whole time. Train the row Training 0 % ID 976 Illustration: the demonstration table is not really trained, so the “learned” numbers here are made up. After training: both are frozen When the trained model reads any sentence, the same ID always gives the same starting vector. Same starting vector, different meaning “bank” means different things in these two sentences, yet the tokenizer gives both the same ID, so both read the same row. Attention is what changes them afterwards, by mixing in the words around them. I ·sat ·on ·the ·river ·bank . entries.heading: The whole text: a matrix, then one vector
entries.text: Do steps 1 to 5 for every token and stack the results: 6 rows × 8 columns. This matrix is what the transformer actually reads. Click a row to select its token. Token d 1 d 2 d 3 d 4 d 5 d 6 d 7 d 8 The ·ship ·reached ·the ·port . Average each column (mean pooling) to get one vector for the whole text. For column d1: ( +0.11 +0.44 +0.26 −0.07 −2.21 −0.84 ) ÷ 6 = −0.39 −0.39 d 1 −0.20 d 2 +0.08 d 3 +0.64 d 4 +0.22 d 5 +1.14 d 6 −0.30 d 7 +0.83 d 8 Sentence-embedding models, like the ones RAG uses to search documents, also end with one vector per text, often by averaging. They average the vectors after the model’s layers have mixed in the meaning of the neighbours; here we average the input vectors to show the idea. In a real model The table is learned during training, starting from random numbers like these. After training, pieces used in similar ways end up with similar rows. Rows are much longer: Qwen2.5-0.5B uses 896 numbers per token and Llama 3 8B uses 4,096. So the table is huge: about 200,000 rows × thousands of numbers. It is one of the largest single blocks of weights in the model. After the starting vectors

entries.heading: What happens next: tokens share clues inside the Transformer
entries.text: Each word helps shape the meaning of the sentence, and the sentence helps shape the meaning of each word. In “The ship reached the port”, ship gives port a clue that it means a harbor; “the” and “reached” show that ship is a vessel doing something; and reached tells us what happened: the vessel arrived at the harbor. Each token starts with its learned vector; in every layer it picks up clues from the other tokens, and the next layer works with the updated vectors. 1 Each token gets a Query, a Key and a Value Think of every token as a card. Each card holds its text, its position and its current vector. From that vector the model calculates three smaller vectors: the Query looks for clues, the Key helps match, and the Value carries a clue that can be shared. Query looks for clues Key helps match Value carries a clue The 1 ·ship 2 ·reached 3 ·the 4 ·port 5 . 6 Click a token to make it the one asking. Click a bar below to see the match with that token. SHIP answering (its Key and Value are used)

The Values, mixed by these shares, give “port” a clue of [0.42, 0.21, 0.35]. It is added to its vector, so the next layer works with an updated “port” that knows about its neighbours. Positions (1–6) say where a token sits; they are separate from the token IDs the tokenizer assigns. The IDs are real; the Query, Key and Value numbers are made up to show the idea. Real models learn them and use many attention heads, each looking for different clues. This is encoder-style attention, where every token can look at every other one; GPT-style models let each token look only at the tokens before it.

entries.heading: 2Self-attention, step by step: how “it” finds “cat”
entries.title: 2 Self-attention, step by step: how “it” finds “cat”
entries.text: Read “The cat sat on the mat because it was tired.” You know at once that “it” is the cat, but the word “it” does not contain that information. At the start, each token is just a vector that does not yet capture its meaning in the sentence. Attention lets each token gather information from the tokens before it and update its representation based on what matters. This is how GPT-style models such as large language models read. The 976 ·cat 9059 ·sat 10139 ·on 402 ·the 290 ·mat 2450 ·because 2236 ·it 480 ·was 673 ·tired 25920 . 13 1 Query, Key and Value Each token’s vector is multiplied by three learned weight matrices to give a Query (what the token is looking for), a Key (what it can be matched on) and a Value (the information it can pass along). The Query of “it” might be looking for the thing it refers to. 2 Compare Query with Keys The Query of “it” is compared with the Keys of the tokens before it, including its own, using a dot product. A stronger match gives a higher score. Tokens after “it” are not visible yet. 3 Softmax: weights that add up to 1 The scores pass through softmax and become weights that add up to 1. Here “cat” gets a high weight and most other tokens get much smaller ones. 4 Weighted sum of Values The model takes a weighted sum of the Value vectors and adds it to the representation of “it”. “it” is no longer just a generic pronoun: it now carries information from its context. 5 Every token does it: self-attention Every token sends a Query, compares it with the Keys of the tokens before it, and gathers from their Values. The result is an attention pattern of who attends to whom. It is called self-attention because the sentence attends to itself: the Queries, Keys and Values all come from the same tokens. 6 Several heads in parallel Transformers run several attention heads in parallel. Each head learns its own weights for making Queries, Keys and Values, so different heads capture different relationships between tokens. “it” starting vector × W Q → Query what it is looking for: the thing it refers to × W K → Key what it can be matched on × W V → Value the information it can pass along Previous step Next step

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: It helps the model connect related words, even when they are far apart in a sentence. It lets the meaning a token represents change with its context.

entries.heading: The big picture
entries.text: At its core, attention lets each token gather the information it needs from context, turning isolated representations into ones that reflect the meaning of the sentence. Token IDs are real (o200k_base); the scores and weights are illustrative, since a real model learns them. Panel 1 shows encoder-style attention, where every token sees every other; this panel shows the GPT-style version, where each token sees only itself and the tokens before it. Explanation based on Data Science Foundry’s short video on attention (Instagram) . 3 Does position matter? Yes What is the capital of Oman? asks for a city Oman is the capital of what? asks for whatever Oman is the capital of Almost the same words, but their order changes their roles. In the original Transformer a position vector is added to each token’s starting vector (you saw it above), so attention can use both what a token is and where it sits. 4 How a Transformer answers a question What 4827 ·is 382 ·the 290 ·capital 9029 ·of 328 ·Oman 126197 ? 30 1 Tokenize The tokenizer cuts the question into tokens and gives each one its ID. 2 Look up embeddings Each ID selects one row of the embedding table: its starting vector. 3 Add position Position information tells the model where each token sits. 4 Share clues (attention + feed-forward) Across many layers, attention lets tokens pick up clues from one another, such as the link between “capital” and “Oman”. The feed-forward network then refines each vector. 5 Predict the next token The output weights score every token in the vocabulary. The model picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats. How does it link “capital” and “Oman”? One attention head might work like this: Query CAPITAL’s Query is like asking: “Which country are we talking about?” Key That Query is compared with the Key on every token card. OMAN’s Key is a strong match, so it gets a high attention weight. Value OMAN’s Value then adds information to CAPITAL’s updated vector, which now carries a clue about whose capital the question asks for. The cards only contain numbers. The questions above are a way to explain what those numbers can do. What a head looks for depends on what it learned in training. Step 5, repeated: the answer is built one token at a time Generate One token Press Generate. Each time, the model reads the question plus the answer so far and predicts one more token. The original Transformer has an encoder that reads the question and a decoder that writes the answer. GPT-style models such as GPT-4o use one decoder stack for both, but the steps are the same. The order of the calculations comes from the model’s design; the numbers they use come from its learned weights. 5 The Transformer’s weight workbook The model’s weight files are like a workbook (think of a spreadsheet file) full of learned numbers, with different sheets for different jobs. Click a sheet to see where the model uses it. Embedding table Attention weights Feed-forward weights (MLP) Normalization weights Output weights Attention weights : Help tokens share clues. In “The ship reached the port”, ship helps port mean a harbor. Look up embeddings every layer Attention every layer Feed-forward every layer Normalize Score next token The model design sets the order. The workbook supplies the weights. A simplified picture: real models keep separate attention, feed-forward and normalization weights for every layer, and normalization is applied around attention and feed-forward rather than as one separate step. 6 How Transformer layers work together Each layer is like a workshop station with the same two tools: attention, which lets each token pick up clues from other tokens, and a feed-forward network (MLP), which then processes each token’s vector on its own. Every station has its own learned weights and receives the vectors the station before it updated. Send the vectors through The ship reached the port . Starting vectors The ·ship ·reached ·the ·port .
