Lesson 10 of 12 How does a language model choose the next word? Watch a tiny transformer turn words into numbers, look back with attention, and predict the next token. Hide intro Continue

entries.heading: The ideas
entries.text: Text is cut into tokens, and every token becomes a vector of numbers (an embedding). Attention is a weighted sum: the current token decides how much to read from each earlier token. A small network of the neurons you already know (the MLP) transforms the result. Softmax turns scores into probabilities; training lowers the cross-entropy loss of the correct next token.

entries.heading: Try this
entries.text: Click each stage button (Tokens, Embeddings, Attention, MLP, Softmax, Backprop) and read what it does to this prompt. Click an earlier token and see which words it attends to. Press Backprop one step, then Trace top link to follow one error value back through the chain rule. Transformer playground

entries.heading: How a language model guesses the next token
entries.text: Type a few words. Then follow them down the page through the six stages every language model uses, from plain text to a prediction, and watch the model learn from its mistake. Every number on this page is calculated live by a real, tiny transformer. Prompt Predict next Generate 8 Try: “ the cat ran to the ” “ the dog ran to the ” “ the dog sat on the ” “ the cat saw the ” the cat ran to the mat 100% sure Stage 1 of 6

entries.heading: Tokens
entries.text: How does text become numbers? 5 tokens the 9 cat 1 ran 6 to 10 the 9

entries.heading: The whole vocabulary: every token this model knows
entries.text: 0 . 1 cat 2 dog 3 log 4 mat 5 on 6 ran 7 sat 8 saw 9 the 10 to

entries.heading: The story it learned them from
entries.text: the cat sat on the mat . the dog sat on the log . the cat saw the dog . the dog saw the cat . the cat ran to the mat . the dog ran to the log .

entries.heading: What happens
entries.text: A model cannot read letters. Your text is cut into pieces called tokens , and each token is replaced by its number in the model’s vocabulary. From here on, the model only ever sees numbers.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: This tiny model knows just the 11 tokens of its story, so every other word is invisible to it. Real language models use tens of thousands of word pieces, which lets them spell any word. Try it. Type a word that is not in the story, such as zebra , and press Predict next. See what the model does with it. Stage 2 of 6

entries.heading: Embeddings
entries.text: What does a word look like to the model? 16 numbers per token Looking at the 1 cat 2 ran 3 to 4 the 5 Token row for “ the ” (row 9 of the token table) 16 numbers · hover to read + Position row (place 5 in the sentence) 16 numbers · hover to read = x, the vector the model reads for “ the ” 16 numbers · hover to read positive number negative number brighter = larger

entries.heading: What happens
entries.text: Each token number picks one row from a table of learned numbers: its embedding . A second row for its position in the sentence is added. The sum, a list of 16 numbers, is what the model works with.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: These numbers begin random and are learned by backpropagation, exactly like the weights of a neuron. Tokens that are used in similar ways end up with similar rows, and that is how meaning gets stored as numbers. Try it. The prompt contains “the” more than once. Select each one: the token row is identical, only the small position row changes. Stage 3 of 6

entries.heading: Attention
entries.text: Which earlier words does this word read? reads “ to ” 52% the 1 cat 2 ran 3 to 4 the 5 query Light moves from the tokens the query reads into the query itself. Values flowing into the query Arc width = attention weight Last 12 tokens q = x·Wq k = x·Wk v = x·Wv score = q·k / √ 16 a = softmax(score) c = Σ a·v

entries.heading: What “the” reads
entries.text: Trace top link # Token score (q · k) weight Share Trace 1 the -4.62 0.002 2 cat 0.66 0.445 3 ran -2.63 0.017 4 to 0.80 0.515 5 the -2.40 0.021 context c, the weighted sum this token collected 16 numbers · hover to read Click a token to make it the query. Click a bolt or an arc to trace the loss back through every stage.

entries.heading: What happens
entries.text: The token “ the ” looks back at the tokens before it. It gives each one a score , and softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to 1 . It then collects a weighted sum of what those tokens offer: the context .

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: Attention is how a word uses the rest of its sentence. It is a weighted sum, the same operation as inside a neuron, but the weights are calculated fresh from the tokens themselves instead of being fixed. Try it. Click “cat” in the picture. The tokens to its right fade, because a model may never look ahead at words it has not written yet. Stage 4 of 6

entries.heading: MLP
entries.text: What does the model do with what it gathered? 20 of 32 neurons on Input: token vector + what attention gathered 16 numbers · hover to read × weights, + bias, ReLU 32 hidden neurons · ReLU 20 on · 12 off × weights, + bias, then added to the input Finished vector: everything the model knows at this position 16 numbers · hover to read h = x + attention n = ReLU(h·W1 + b1) out = h + n·W2 + b2

entries.heading: What happens
entries.text: What attention gathered is added to the token’s own vector, then passed through a small network of ordinary neurons: multiply by weights, add a bias, apply ReLU. Its result is added back on top. Right now 20 of its 32 neurons are switched on.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: This is the network from lesson 1, unchanged. Attention gathers information from other words; the MLP decides what to do with it. A large model simply repeats this pair of steps dozens of times. Try it. Switch between the “cat” and “dog” examples and watch which neurons light up. Different neurons respond to different situations. Stage 5 of 6

entries.heading: Softmax
entries.text: How do numbers become the next word? “ mat ” 100% mat most likely next token 100% of the probability In the story mat matched The real next token got 100% . Its loss is 0.001 . Temperature 1.0 Low = careful and repetitive. High = surprising. Append top token Sample one token score probability mat 19.7 100% on 12.8 0.1% cat 7.4 0.0% log 6.2 0.0% to 5.3 0.0% sat 3.9 0.0% ran -0.6 0.0% . -5.2 0.0% the -12.8 0.0% probability = e^(score ÷ temperature) ÷ sum of all e^(score ÷ temperature)

entries.heading: What happens
entries.text: A final layer turns the finished vector into one score for every token in the vocabulary. Softmax converts the 11 scores into probabilities that add up to 100%. The next token is then picked from that list.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: A language model never outputs a word. It outputs a probability for every token it knows, and choosing from that list, one token at a time, is how it writes whole sentences. Try it. Slide the temperature up and watch the bars flatten: unlikely tokens get a real chance. Then press Sample one a few times. Stage 6 of 6

entries.heading: Learn
entries.text: How does the model get better? loss 0.001 This token 0.001 Whole story 0.115 loss = −ln( p of “ mat ” ) = −ln( 0.999 ) = 0.001 Embeddings token and position tables 0.0264 Attention query, key, value weights 0.0336 MLP two layers of neurons 0.0397 Output one score per token 0.0265 Loss the error starts here 0.001 The error starts at the loss on the right and travels left. Each bar is the size of the gradient for that group of weights: how strongly this one token wants them to change. Backprop one step Train 10 steps Reset model

entries.heading: Loss of the whole story after each training step
entries.text: Press a training button to draw the loss curve. One step is one round of gradient descent over the whole story. Lower is better; Reset model brings back the saved classroom weights.

entries.heading: What happens
entries.text: The model’s probability for the correct token is turned into a loss : −ln(probability). Certain and right gives almost 0; certain and wrong gives a large number. Backpropagation then carries that error back through every stage above and nudges every weight.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: This loop is all that “training a language model” means: predict the next token, measure the loss, send the error back, adjust 2,667 weights a little. Real models repeat it over billions of words. Try it. Choose “the dog ran to the”. The model is confidently wrong, so the loss and the error bars are large. Then press Train 10 steps and watch them shrink.

Lesson 11 of 12 How do you teach a ready-made model your own subject? See how fine-tuning adds a small set of new weights beside frozen ones, and how quantization, QLoRA and Unsloth make it fit on an ordinary GPU. Hide intro Continue

entries.heading: The ideas
entries.text: Fine-tuning continues the training of a foundation model on your own examples. LoRA freezes the original weights and trains two small matrices, A and B, beside them. Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits, so a large model fits in a small memory. QLoRA is both together: a frozen 4-bit base with trainable adapters. Unsloth is the library that runs it.

entries.heading: Try this
entries.text: In the LoRA part, train with rank 1, then rank 2, and watch the frozen weights stay unchanged. In the quantization part, go from 8 bits to 2, then compare even spacing with NF4 at 4 bits. In the QLoRA part, find the largest model that fits on a 16 GB GPU. Fine-tuning lab

entries.heading: Teach a ready-made model your own subject
entries.text: Sixteen short parts in six chapters, in the order a real project follows: from the base model and its data, through LoRA, quantization, QLoRA and Unsloth, to training, evaluation and RAG in depth, and then two real student projects that share one recipe, one of them with computer vision. Each part has an animation to watch, tools to try and a card to remember. Search the lab Ctrl K Reference sheet Part 1 of 16

entries.heading: Why fine-tune
entries.text: What does a ready-made model not know? base → specialist Try it. Switch between the three situations. In which one did the model gain knowledge, and in which one did it only gain a habit? College helpdesk A fixed report format A course’s own vocabulary When is the registration deadline for the spring term?

entries.heading: Base model
entries.text: I don’t have information about your specific institution. Registration deadlines vary, so please check your college’s website or contact the registrar’s office.

entries.heading: After fine-tuning
entries.text: Registration for the spring term closes on 15 January. Register in the student portal under Registration → Spring. After that date you need written approval from the Registrar. The base model is polite but empty: it never read your college’s rules. The fine-tuned model was trained on a few hundred of the helpdesk’s real questions and answers. (An illustration written for this lesson, not a live model.)

entries.heading: Fine-tuning = extra lessons
entries.text: A pre-trained model is a very well-read general student. Fine-tuning gives focused extra lessons on your subject, on top of what it already knows. See part 3

entries.heading: LoRA = sticky notes
entries.text: The model is a printed textbook that is never changed. LoRA writes small sticky notes and corrections on top. You can keep the notes separate, or print a new edition with them merged in. See part 5

entries.heading: Quantization = a smaller photo file
entries.text: Like saving a high-resolution photo as a smaller file: it still looks almost the same, but now it fits on your phone. With 4-bit, a big model fits on one consumer GPU. See part 6

entries.heading: Why fine-tune
entries.text: What does a ready-made model not know? base → specialist 1

entries.heading: Why fine-tune
entries.text: base model + your examples → specialist Fine-tuning continues the training of a model that already knows language, on your own examples. It teaches a subject, a format or a way of answering; it starts from open weights, not from zero. It is not always needed: try prompting first, and use RAG for new facts. Common mistake: “You must fine-tune to add knowledge.” New facts and documents usually belong in RAG.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: A base (foundation) model knows language and general knowledge, but nothing about your college, your format, or your course. Fine-tuning is extra training on your own examples, starting from the weights it already has.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: Training a model from nothing needs months and millions. Starting from open weights, a small team can build a specialist in an afternoon.

entries.heading: Teach a ready-made model your own subject
entries.text: Sixteen short parts in six chapters, in the order a real project follows: from the base model and its data, through LoRA, quantization, QLoRA and Unsloth, to training, evaluation and RAG in depth, and then two real student projects that share one recipe, one of them with computer vision. Each part has an animation to watch, tools to try and a card to remember. Search the lab Ctrl K Reference sheet Part 2 of 16

entries.heading: Key words
entries.text: Which words link the whole process? 8 words, 1 loop Fine-tuning uses a handful of words again and again: parameter, frozen, trainable, activation, loss, gradient, optimizer, batch and epoch. They are not separate topics: they are the steps of one loop that repeats until the model fits the examples. Watch it happen

entries.heading: Input
entries.text: Huge amounts of text (books, websites, code) used by the model’s makers, for example the Qwen team, during the original pre-training. This happened long before your project, over weeks of computing.

entries.heading: Processing
entries.text: Pre-training adjusted billions of numbers again and again, so that the model got better and better at predicting the next word.

entries.heading: Output
entries.text: The learned parameters (weights and biases), published as an open-weight model file. In our tiny example, one neuron of it: w₁ = 0.5, w₂ = 0.4, b = 0.2. w = [0.5, 0.4] · b = 0.2 Step 2 receives these parameters. Go to step 2 To keep the numbers easy, this example uses one neuron and a direct adjustment Δ. In a real model Δ = B·A for whole matrices, the input is tokens, the loss is cross-entropy and a batch holds many examples, but the order of the steps is exactly the same.

entries.heading: Key words
entries.text: Which words link the whole process? 8 words, 1 loop Try it. Start with the neuron: check that 2 × 0.5 + 3 × 0.4 + 0.2 = 2.4. Then train it “the LoRA way” and watch “original parameters changed” stay at 0. Finally play the loop.

entries.heading: What is a parameter? Look inside one neuron
entries.text: Parameters are the numbers a model learns. There are two kinds: weights (w), which set how strongly each input counts, and biases (b), an extra number added before the activation function. Explore the neuron Train every parameter Train the LoRA way x₁ 2.0 x₂ 3.0 w₁ = 0.50 w₂ = 0.40 b = 0.20 Σ z = 2.40 activation f(z) z = ( 2.0 × 0.50 ) + ( 3.0 × 0.40 ) + 0.20 = 2.40 x₁ 2.00 x₂ 3.00 w₁ 0.50 w₂ 0.40 b 0.20

entries.heading: From 3 parameters to billions
entries.text: One neuron 3 2 weights + 1 bias One weight matrix 16.8 M 4,096 × 4,096 weights (+ 4,096 biases, if it has them) One transformer layer 227.8 M seven matrices for attention and the MLP The whole 8B model 8.2 B 36 layers, plus the vocabulary What LoRA trains (r = 16) 47.2 M 0.58% of the model; everything else is frozen Zoom out The bars use a logarithmic scale: each step to the right is ten times more. If you wrote down one parameter of the 8B model every second, it would take about 260 years.

entries.heading: Parameters are not a file of facts
entries.text: Al-Bar’ah is a dance from Dhofar Muscat is the capital of Oman Frankincense grows in Dhofar

entries.heading: A database: one fact, one row
entries.text: Al-Bar’ah is a dance from Dhofar Muscat is the capital of Oman Frankincense grows in Dhofar The fact is written in one place. You can find it, read it and edit it.

entries.heading: A model: patterns spread over many numbers
entries.text: No single number holds the fact. Many numbers take part, and the same numbers also take part in other facts (white outline). That is why you cannot edit one fact by changing one weight. The most important point for students: parameters are not files that contain written facts. They are numbers that cooperate inside the network to represent the patterns the model learned. LoRA changes the model’s behaviour by training a relatively small number of new parameters instead of retraining billions of original ones. The cell patterns are an illustration of the idea, not a measurement from a real model.

entries.heading: Key words
entries.text: Which words link the whole process? 8 words, 1 loop 2

entries.heading: Key words
entries.text: z = x₁w₁ + x₂w₂ + b Parameters are learned numbers: weights (w) and biases (b). Training is one loop: forward → loss → gradient → update → next batch. Frozen means not updated. It does not mean inactive. Common mistake: “The model stores facts in its parameters like a file.” Knowledge is a pattern spread over many numbers.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: Fine-tuning uses a handful of words again and again: parameter, frozen, trainable, activation, loss, gradient, optimizer, batch and epoch. They are not separate topics: they are the steps of one loop that repeats until the model fits the examples.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: The most important sentence of the lesson: frozen means not updated. It does not mean inactive. The original weights calculate every answer; only the small adapter learns.

entries.heading: messages
entries.text: The whole conversation, as a list of turns.

entries.heading: role
entries.text: Who speaks: "system" (optional instructions), "user" (the question) or "assistant" (the answer to learn).

entries.heading: content
entries.text: The text of that turn, in UTF-8, so Arabic is stored as it is. When to use it: Question-and-answer or chat data for instruction-tuned models. TRL’s SFTTrainer and Unsloth read it directly and apply the model’s chat template for you. The second line adds an optional system turn. A conversation can also have several user/assistant turns. Whatever the format, before training it becomes this text (Qwen’s chat template): <|im_start|>user What is Al-Bar’ah? <|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant Al-Bar’ah is a performing art from the Dhofari valleys of Oman that combines dance, music and poetry. <|im_end|> Every document ends up as text. entries.heading: From documents to JSONL
entries.text: document → text → pairs → JSONL → tokens JSONL: one complete JSON object per line, in UTF-8. Split by source (about 80 / 10 / 10), never by random lines. Mask the prompt and train on the answer; check max_seq_length does not cut answers. Common mistake: “Valid JSONL means good data.” JSONL is only a format; truth needs expert review.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: Every source, a PDF, a recording or a scanned page, ends up as text. The text is cleaned, described, turned into reviewed question–answer pairs, and saved as JSONL: one complete JSON object per line. At training time each line is put into the model’s chat template and cut into tokens.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: The examples are the lesson. JSONL is only the box they travel in: it guarantees neither truth nor coverage. A few hundred clean, reviewed, well-split pairs teach more than thousands of careless ones.

entries.heading: What is updated
entries.text: Added low-rank matrices A and B

entries.heading: Base weights
entries.text: Frozen (usually 16-bit)

entries.heading: Typical purpose
entries.text: Compact adapters for a domain or a task

entries.heading: Memory to train
entries.text: ≈ 21 GB

entries.heading: What you save
entries.text: ≈ 90 MB the adapter only Frozen means not updated. It does not mean inactive. Blue layers still compute every answer; they just do not change.

entries.heading: Quantization is not pruning
entries.text: quantization 16 weights, fewer bits each pruning some weights removed Quantization stores the same weights in fewer bits (an approximation). Pruning deletes weights or connections. QLoRA uses quantization: a 27B model is still 27B.

entries.heading: Fine-tuning is not retrieval (RAG)
entries.text: examples → weights change → answer question → find passages → answer + source Fine-tuning changes learned behaviour: terms, style, careful answers. RAG fetches source passages at answer time and changes no weights: best when an answer must be tied to a source. They work together; TurathAI uses both.

entries.heading: Four ways to fine-tune
entries.text: Which weights should learn? full · partial · LoRA · QLoRA 4

entries.heading: Four ways to fine-tune
entries.text: full · partial · LoRA · QLoRA Full fine-tuning updates every weight; partial updates chosen layers. LoRA freezes the base and trains small added matrices A and B. QLoRA is LoRA on a base stored in 4-bit. Common mistake: “Quantization removes weights.” That is pruning. Quantization keeps every weight with fewer bits.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: Full fine-tuning updates every weight. Partial fine-tuning updates chosen layers. LoRA freezes every original weight and adds small new matrices that learn. QLoRA does the same with the frozen base stored in 4-bit.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: Frozen weights keep everything the model already knows, and training a fraction of a percent needs a fraction of the memory. Neither method guarantees perfect recall of facts: data, settings and evaluation decide that.

entries.heading: LoRA
entries.text: How are the new weights added? W + B·A LoRA adds two thin matrices, A and B, beside the frozen matrix W. The layer’s output becomes W·x + B·(A·x). B starts at zero, so at first nothing changes. Training then moves only A and B until B·A equals the change the task needs. Watch it happen

entries.heading: Why B starts at zero (and not both)
entries.text: The same adapter trained for 150 steps, starting three different ways. These are real runs in your browser.

entries.heading: A random, B zero
entries.text: starts like the base model? yes loss : 2.01 → 0.01 Starts exactly at the base model, then learns.

entries.heading: Both zero
entries.text: starts like the base model? yes loss : 2.01 → 2.01 Stuck: with A = 0 and B = 0 every gradient is zero, so nothing ever moves.

entries.heading: Both random
entries.text: starts like the base model? no loss : 3.28 → 0.04 It learns, but starts from noise: before any training its answers are already worse than the base model, and it stays behind.

entries.heading: LoRA
entries.text: How are the new weights added? W + B·A 5

entries.heading: LoRA
entries.text: y = W·x + (α/r)·B(A·x) A is r × in, B is out × r: 1,000 × 1,000 at r = 8 trains 16,000 numbers (1.6%). A starts random, B starts at zero, so training starts exactly from the base model. After training, merge once: W′ = W + s·B·A, or keep the adapter as a small file. Common mistake: “LoRA means a low number of adapters.” It means Low-Rank Adaptation.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: LoRA adds two thin matrices, A and B, beside the frozen matrix W. The layer’s output becomes W·x + B·(A·x). B starts at zero, so at first nothing changes. Training then moves only A and B until B·A equals the change the task needs.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: A new skill usually needs only a few directions of change, not every number. The rank r is how many directions the adapter is allowed: too few and it cannot fit; enough and it matches with far fewer numbers.

entries.heading: Quantization
entries.text: How does a big model fit in a small memory? 32 bits → 4 bits A weight is normally stored in 32 or 16 bits. entries.heading: The photo picture of quantization
entries.text: Bits per colour 8 4 3 2 1 original · 8 bits per colour saved with 4 bits · 16 shades per colour · file 50% At 4 bits the picture is half the size and still clearly the same scene. That is the bet of 4-bit quantization: much less memory, a small loss of detail.

entries.heading: Quantization
entries.text: How does a big model fit in a small memory? 32 bits → 4 bits 6

entries.heading: Quantization
entries.text: memory = parameters × bits ÷ 8 4 bits name only 16 levels; each weight is rounded to the nearest one. NF4 packs its levels near zero, where most weights are. One scale (absmax) is stored per block of 64 weights. Common mistake: “Fewer bits means fewer weights.” The count stays the same; each weight just takes less memory.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: A weight is normally stored in 32 or 16 bits. Quantization keeps a short list of allowed values (levels), rounds each weight to the nearest one, and stores only that level’s number. With 4 bits there are 16 levels.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: Memory is the wall. An 8B model is about 15 GB at 16-bit and under 4 GB at 4-bit, which is the difference between needing a server and using a free cloud GPU. The price is a small rounding error.

Base model 4-bit · frozen + LoRA adapters 16-bit · learning Answer and loss error flows back The error travels back through the frozen 4-bit weights, which are read but not changed, and lands only on the adapters.

entries.heading: The order matters
entries.text: QLoRA LoRA, then quantize later 1 Load the base in 4-bit (or quantize it while loading) 4 -bit 2 Freeze it and attach LoRA adapters 4 -bit 3 Train the adapters; the 4-bit base takes part in every calculation 4 -bit 4 Save the adapters and the exact base they belong to 4 -bit The base is quantized for the training run itself. That is what makes it QLoRA, and what saves memory while training.

entries.heading: Stored in 4-bit, calculated in 16-bit
entries.text: 4-bit stored codes + scale 1101 0111 1000 … bfloat16 rebuilt for this layer only 0.42 −0.13 0.07 … W·x + s·B(A·x) computed in 16-bit output temporary weights thrown away Play the flow again NF4 — the 4-bit format whose levels sit where weights usually are. Double quantization — the scales themselves are quantized too, saving about 0.4 bits per weight. Paged optimizers — optimizer memory can spill to the computer’s RAM during short memory spikes instead of crashing. QLoRA does not mean every number or every calculation is 4-bit. 4 bits is only how the frozen base is stored; the adapters train in 16-bit.

entries.heading: A transparent memory sum: a 27B model
entries.text: Raw weight storage = number of parameters × bits per parameter ÷ 8. (Decimal GB: 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes.) 32 -bit 27 B × 4 bytes 108 GB 16 -bit 27 B × 2 bytes 54 GB 4 -bit 27 B × 0.5 bytes 13.5 GB 13.5 GB is the raw weights, not a GPU budget. Training also needs: quantization constants (scales) parts kept in 16-bit adapters + their gradients optimizer state activations temporary buffers Measure real use with a short pilot run. Do not conclude that a 13.5 GB GPU can train this model.

entries.heading: QLoRA
entries.text: What happens when we combine the two? 4-bit base + adapters 7

entries.heading: QLoRA
entries.text: 4-bit frozen base + 16-bit LoRA adapters Order: load the base in 4-bit, freeze it, attach adapters, train. Stored in 4-bit, calculated in 16-bit (bfloat16). 27B: 54 GB at 16-bit, 13.5 GB at 4-bit for the raw weights, which is not a full GPU budget. Common mistake: “QLoRA compresses the model after training.” The base is already 4-bit during training.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: QLoRA is the two ideas together: load the base model quantized to 4-bit and frozen, then train LoRA adapters beside it at normal precision. The 4-bit weights are only read; the learning is stored in the adapters.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: Quantization shrinks what you load; LoRA shrinks what you train. Together they bring fine-tuning of a multi-billion-weight model down to a single consumer GPU, with results close to full fine-tuning.

Heritage accuracy

entries.heading: Fine-tuning, RAG, or both?
entries.text: What goes in the library, and what in the lessons? library + storyteller RAG lets the model look up relevant material before it answers; fine-tuning teaches it how you want it to answer. Think of an open-book exam: RAG is the open book, fine-tuning is the coaching. RAG is the library: all the real stories, searched at answer time, with their sources. Fine-tuning is the lessons: a smaller set of examples that teach the model how to tell those stories, use the retrieved context, cite it, and admit when a story is missing. entries.heading: Do you need fine-tuning? Pick a situation
entries.text: Simple questions, general knowledge New facts or documents A new style, tone, format or persona Follow specific rules or an output structure Deep adaptation to a domain

entries.heading: Usually enough
entries.text: Prompting with good instructions

entries.heading: When fine-tuning helps a lot
entries.text: Not needed. The base model already knows this. A clear instruction is enough. Fine-tuning is not always required. Use it when the model must reliably behave in a new way. Full fine-tuning of every weight is almost never necessary.

entries.heading: Is one enough? Answer three questions
entries.text: Try: TurathAI after testing A museum help desk A passage simplifier Must answers come from your own collection, with references? Yes No With RAG, does the base Qwen already explain the passages well, in the Arabic you want? Yes No Is the job a fixed style or task on a passage the user supplies (for example, “rewrite this in simpler Arabic”)? Yes No not needed for this decision Approach When it may be enough RAG alone Your main goal is to answer from your collection with references, and the base Qwen already explains the material well in Arabic. Fine-tuning alone Your main goal is a consistent style or task, such as rewriting a supplied heritage passage in simpler Arabic for students. RAG + fine-tuning You need source-backed answers, and the base model repeatedly struggles with local expressions, the level of Arabic you want, or how to present differing accounts. You can only answer question 2 honestly by testing. So build RAG first, ask real heritage questions, and use the two checks below. Fine-tuning comes after, only if the tests ask for it.

entries.heading: What each method is good at
entries.text: Fine-tuning only RAG only Both together Natural, culturally appropriate storytelling strong Fine-tuning teaches the voice; a base model reading documents sounds generic. Staying faithful to recorded sources strong A tuned model remembers stories only approximately and can invent details. A clear source for every claim strong Only retrieval knows which document an answer came from. Fewer invented answers strong Tuning can teach it to say “I don’t know”; retrieval gives it something true to say. Rare or very local stories strong A few examples are not enough to learn a story; a library keeps every one. Score: 10 of 10 — the combination is strong where each one alone is weak.

entries.heading: One answer, three ways: who wrote which part?
entries.text: What does ⁨«الجار قبل الدار»⁩ mean, and when do people say it? With both Without RAG Without fine-tuning ⁨«الجار قبل الدار»⁩ Accounts differ (تختلف الروايات): As advice: look at who your neighbours will be before you choose a home [ 1 ] At home: said to children when a neighbour needs help, because the neighbour comes first [ 2 ] Both uses share one idea: good neighbours matter more than a fine house. RAG words, fine-tuned habit The words come from the retrieved passage. Keeping them unchanged, instead of paraphrasing, is a habit the fine-tuning examples taught. Faithful and well told: every claim has a source, and the answer reads the way you taught it.

entries.heading: How train.jsonl is applied in fine-tuning
entries.text: train.jsonl All your teaching examples, one per line. Load the file load_dataset("json") reads every line as one example. Template + tokens Each conversation is put in the chat template and cut into tokens. Learn the answer only The user part is shown but masked; the model is trained to produce the assistant part. Update LoRA only Only the small LoRA weights change. The 4-bit base stays frozen. Play the flow again from datasets import load_dataset from trl import SFTTrainer from unsloth.chat_templates import train_on_responses_only dataset = load_dataset("json", data_files = "train.jsonl", split = "train") trainer = SFTTrainer(model = model, # 4-bit base + LoRA adapters train_dataset = dataset, # each line = one example ...) trainer = train_on_responses_only(trainer, ...) # learn the assistant part only trainer.train() # only the LoRA weights change The “...” stand for settings such as the tokenizer, the chat-template markers and the training arguments. Check the Unsloth documentation for the exact arguments of your version.

entries.heading: How the vector search finds the right story
entries.text: How did people prepare for the monsoon? What did they do when the wind was very strong? Is there a story about a fox? entries.heading: A sensible order of work
entries.text: 1 Build and test RAG first Good chunks, good search, and the source shown with every answer. This alone is already a useful, safe system. 2 Then fine-tune for behaviour QLoRA on a smaller, curated set: the storyteller’s voice, using the retrieved context, citing it, and saying “I don’t have this story”. 3 Compare three systems Pure RAG, pure fine-tuning, and the combination, on the same unseen questions. Then evaluate faithfulness to the sources, the storytelling tone, and how often it honestly says “I don’t have this story” (see part 10 for the full evaluation). For TurathAI (Part 14): combining fine-tuning and RAG is a solid, defensible choice. Keep the full archive in RAG, and let the fine-tuning set teach the storyteller’s voice, citing and honest “not found” answers, rather than asking the model to memorize every story.

entries.heading: Fine-tuning, RAG, or both?
entries.text: What goes in the library, and what in the lessons? library + storyteller 11

entries.heading: Fine-tuning, RAG, or both?
entries.text: RAG = the library · fine-tuning = the storyteller All real stories go into RAG; 5–20% curated teaching examples go into fine-tuning. Write training examples as question + retrieved context → answer with the source. Vector search finds by meaning; when nothing matches, the model should say so. Common mistake: “Put the same stories in both.” The model then mixes memorized and retrieved versions.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: RAG lets the model look up relevant material before it answers; fine-tuning teaches it how you want it to answer. Think of an open-book exam: RAG is the open book, fine-tuning is the coaching. RAG is the library: all the real stories, searched at answer time, with their sources. Fine-tuning is the lessons: a smaller set of examples that teach the model how to tell those stories, use the retrieved context, cite it, and admit when a story is missing.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: Fine-tuning alone sounds good but can invent details and gives no source. RAG alone is accurate but sounds generic. Together they are faithful and natural, which is what a heritage project needs. But start with RAG: add fine-tuning only if testing shows the model still struggles with local language, terminology, or differing versions of a story.

entries.heading: RAG in depth
entries.text: How are documents stored, sliced and searched? documents → chunks → vectors → answers RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) gives a language model an open book. Once, offline, every trusted document is extracted, cleaned, cut into chunks, turned into tokens and then into an embedding vector, and stored with its text and metadata in a vector database. Then, for every question, the question is embedded the same way, the nearest chunks are found, filtered, reranked and placed in the prompt with their sources, and the model answers from them and cites them. 1 · Indexing: documents into the archive 2 · Answering: a question finds its sources

entries.heading: What is RAG?
entries.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a way of building an AI assistant in which, before the language model writes an answer, the system searches a collection of trusted documents, picks the passages that best match the question, and gives them to the model as evidence. The model answers from that evidence and cites it. Closed-book exam (no RAG) Open-book exam (RAG) “What is frankincense resin used for in Dhofar?” “In Dhofar the dried resin is burned as incense and used in traditional practices [1]; it is collected through small cuts in the bark [2].” Specific, checkable, cited. The model answers from passages it was handed a second ago.

entries.heading: Why we need it
entries.text: Knowledge the model never saw A model knows only what was in its training data, up to a cut-off date. Local heritage stories and Dhofar flora books were never in it. RAG brings your own documents to the model at the moment of the question. Fewer invented answers Asked about something it does not know, a model often writes a fluent, confident guess: a hallucination. The answer is grounded in retrieved passages; if nothing relevant is found, the rules say “not in my sources”. Every claim has a source Facts stored inside the weights cannot be traced: no book, no page, no storyteller. Each passage carries its metadata, so the answer can cite “Source A, p. 112” or “story DHF-2018-014”. Update without retraining Teaching a fine-tuned model a new fact means preparing data and training again. Add, correct or delete a document and re-index it. The model is untouched.

entries.heading: Two phases, two times
entries.text: 1 · Indexing (once, offline) 2 · Answering (every question) 1 upload 2 extract 3 clean 4 chunk 5 tokenize 6 embed 7 store RAG and fine-tuning are partners, not rivals: RAG supplies the facts at answer time, fine-tuning teaches the model how to use them. Both student projects use both. Part 11 : Fine-tuning, RAG, or both?

entries.heading: The chunking lab: how to slice a document
entries.text: UTAS-70 · flora entry: Boswellia sacra TurathAI · oral story DHF-2018-014 Fixed size By sentence By section (structure-aware) Cut every N tokens, wherever that falls. Simple and predictable, but it can cut a sentence or a section in half. Chunk size (words) 25 Overlap 0 % · 0 answer Names Description Distribution in Dhofar Uses Note 1 2 3 4 5 6 6 chunks ≈ 33 tokens per chunk ✕ answer in one chunk Test question: How is the resin collected, and what is it used for? The answer is split across chunks 4 and 5. If the search returns only one of them, the model gets half the answer. A balanced size: each chunk is about one idea, and still says what it is about. Chunk 1 Boswellia sacra belongs to the family Burseraceae. In Arabic it is called shajarat al-luban, and in English the frankincense tree. It is a small tree, { "chunk_id" : " U-BS-1 " , "doc" : " Source A, pp. 112–113 " , "section" : " n/a " , "prev" :null, "next" : " U-BS-2 " , "words" :25} Real documents are longer, so real chunks are larger: a common start is 200–500 tokens with 10–20% overlap. Choose with evidence: write 20 test questions, chunk two or three ways, and keep the setting whose top results contain the answers most often. Shaded words are shared with a neighbour (overlap); gold words are the answer.

entries.text: Frankincense resin is burned as incense. The tree’s dried sap is used for perfume and smoke. اللبان يُحرق بخورًا في البيوت. Families stored water before the monsoon rain. The camel crossed the desert at night. 1 Tokens and their IDs ▁Frank 113176 incense 214900 ▁resin 196477 ▁is 6572 ▁burned 212072 ▁as 124764 ▁incense 243383 . 146873 IDs are positions in the vocabulary. They carry no meaning: “resin” and “sap” get unrelated numbers. 2 Embedding model Every layer mixes each token with its context; the token vectors are then averaged into one. 3 The vector (16 of 1,024 numbers shown) [ -0.11, -0.20, 0.19, -0.29 , …]

entries.heading: Cosine similarity: how close is the meaning?
entries.text: Frankincense resin is burned as incense. 1.00 The tree’s dried sap is used for perfume and smoke. 0.98 اللبان يُحرق بخورًا في البيوت. 0.99 Families stored water before the monsoon rain. -0.26 The camel crossed the desert at night. -0.58 The two English sentences about resin share almost no words, and one Arabic sentence shares none, yet their vectors are close. The camel sentence is far away. This is why RAG searches by meaning, not by spelling. The numbers here are computed in your browser to behave like a real multilingual model.

entries.text: After embedding, every chunk’s vector is stored with its text and metadata so it can be searched by meaning. Many tools can do this. They differ in where they run, who operates them, and what search they add on top. Pick a situation to see which option fits. entries.text: { "id" : " T-014-3 " , "text" : " …one passage of the transcript… " , "embedding" : [0.12, -0.08, 0.31, " … 1,024 numbers " ], "source_title" : " Oral collection, Salalah " , "source_type" : " audio transcript " , "recording_timestamp" : " 00:12:40–00:14:05 " , "page" : null, "region" : " Dhofar " , "dialect" : " Dhofari Arabic " , "language" : " ar " } Each searchable record is one passage from a document or a transcript. entries.heading: From retrieved chunks to a cited answer
entries.text: How is the resin collected and used? When does it flower? The prompt the model receives SYSTEM: Answer only from the numbered sources. Cite each claim as [n]. If the sources do not contain the answer, say “My sources do not say.” Reply in the user’s language. Add: for education only. [ 1 ] The dried resin is burned as incense and used in traditional practices. Source A — Flora of Dhofar, p. 113 · U-BS-uses [ 2 ] Small cuts are made in the bark; the sap hardens into tears over several weeks. Field notes 3 — harvest survey · U-BS-harvest The answer The resin is collected through small cuts in the bark, and the sap hardens over several weeks [2] . Once dry, it is burned as incense and used in traditional practices [1] . For education only. [ 1 ] Source A — Flora of Dhofar, p. 113 [ 2 ] Field notes 3 — harvest survey ✓ every claim has a source ✓ nothing from memory ✓ sources exist and match Click a citation number to see the chunk behind it. The application, not the model, turns [1] into the full reference from the metadata, so a reference can never be invented.

entries.text: Did families in Dhofar serve coffee first to guests? [ 1 ] Interview INT-2020-031 · a family in Taqah · 08:10 In our house the guest was given coffee first, then dates. [ 2 ] Interview INT-2022-012 · a family in the mountains · 22:40 My grandmother set out ⁨«الفوالة»⁩ first, and only then poured the coffee. Qwen as it comes Qwen + clearer instructions Fine-tuned Qwen base model + a plain prompt Yes. In Dhofar, coffee is served to guests first, followed by dates [ 1 ] . Generalises one family’s practice to all of Dhofar Drops the second interview, which says the opposite Cites a real source The search worked: both interviews arrived. The writing failed. A polished, confident answer can still be wrong. Sample interviews for teaching, not real archive records.

entries.heading: RAG in the two student projects
entries.text: TurathAI UTAS-70 Documents Transcribed oral stories, UNESCO element files, books and articles on Omani heritage. Flora books, research papers, field notes, herbarium sheets. Extraction Audio → transcript, checked by a second listener; OCR for printed books; dialect words kept. PyMuPDF for digital PDFs; Tesseract OCR (Arabic + English) for scans; page numbers kept. Chunk unit One story, or one scene of a long story. A story is never split mid-scene: its meaning is in the whole. One topic of one species (names, description, distribution, uses), following the book’s headings. Size and overlap About 300–500 tokens per scene, one sentence of overlap between scenes. About 150–300 tokens per topic; overlap rarely needed because topics are self-contained. Linking the pieces story_id, scene number, previous / next scene; the full story is the parent. species key, topic, source and page; the full species entry is the parent. The question comes from The user’s text, often in Arabic or a dialect. The species name from YOLO + the user’s question. Filter before searching Optional: region, category or collection, when the user names one. Always: species = the YOLO name, so another plant cannot answer. Search Hybrid: vectors for meaning + keywords for names such as Al-Bar’ah; Arabic spelling normalised. Vectors within the filtered species, keywords for Latin names; top 3 after reranking. Citation (Story DHF-2018-014, oral collection, Salalah, 2018) (Source A, p. 113) · (Field notes 3) When nothing is found “I don’t have a recorded source for this story.” “My sources do not say. Please check with a botanist.”

entries.heading: The RAG doctor: symptom → cause → fix
entries.text: The answer talks about the wrong plant or story. The answer is only half right. Names such as Al-Bar’ah or Boswellia are not found. It invents an answer when the archive has nothing. An Arabic question finds nothing in English documents. A corrected fact is still answered the old way. Cause Passages from similar items competed freely. Fix Filter by metadata (species, story, region) before ranking. Show me in the lab Measure retrieval and generation separately. Retrieval: for a set of test questions, is the right chunk in the top k (hit rate), and how high (MRR)? Generation: is every sentence supported by its cited chunk (faithfulness), and do the citations point to the right sources?

entries.heading: You tested it. What do you fix first?
entries.text: Ask real questions about proverbs, customs and oral stories, and read the retrieved passages next to each answer. Then pick what you saw. Qwen finds the answer in the passages and explains it faithfully. The app retrieves an unrelated interview, or misses the right one. Right interview, but Qwen repeatedly misreads a Dhofari expression. Right passages, but Qwen mixes up two different accounts. Two interviews about two families become “all families in Dhofar”. The facts are right; you only want a neater format. Keep Qwen + RAG Nothing to change. Improve the archive search Chunking, metadata filters, hybrid search, threshold, missing documents. Clearer instructions + a few examples Rules and worked examples in the prompt. Cheap, instant, no training. try this Fine-tune Qwen Examples that teach the behaviour, when the problem persists. if it persists Try clearer instructions and examples first. If it persists, fine-tune with examples of local expressions in context.

entries.heading: Prove it: a fair test of regular vs fine-tuned Qwen
entries.text: 1 The same questions for both models 2 The same retrieved passages, so only the writer differs 3 Questions held back from training 4 Mark facts and sources, not polish; markers do not know which model wrote which answer Example result A Example result B Qwen + RAG Fine-tuned Qwen + RAG / 40 Facts right 31 37 Cites the correct source 30 38 Says when the evidence is insufficient 18 34 Fine-tuned Qwen is more consistent on all three, above all on admitting when the evidence is insufficient. Here fine-tuning adds accuracy. Illustrative numbers on 40 held-out questions. Run the same test with your own questions; that result is your evidence.

entries.heading: Is a fine-tuned model a good addition? The claim, put precisely
entries.text: The archive preserves the original accounts RAG brings the relevant accounts into the conversation Fine-tuned Qwen explains them in clear Arabic, preserving their local meaning and differences Yes, and this is where it is strongest Every RAG answer is written by a language model. The search step brings excerpts and references; Qwen reads, writes and formats. So how well Qwen reads heritage material shapes every answer. Cultural and linguistic accuracy: local expressions read correctly, each narrator’s wording kept, accounts kept apart, claims limited to the evidence. Saying ⁦⁨«تختلف الروايتان»⁩⁩ and exactly where they differ, because for intangible heritage the differences are part of what is preserved. Be careful with these Fine-tuning is optional, not required: start with Qwen as it comes + RAG. For formatting alone, instructions and a few examples are usually enough. Fine-tuning does not fix retrieval: a missed interview stays missed. A polished answer can still be wrong. Claim the improvement only after the fair test shows it.

entries.heading: RAG in depth
entries.text: How are documents stored, sliced and searched? documents → chunks → vectors → answers 12

entries.heading: RAG in depth
entries.text: documents → chunks → tokens → vectors → search → cited answer Indexing runs once: extract, clean, chunk (200–500 tokens, 10–20% overlap), embed, store vector + text + metadata. Answering runs per question: same tokenizer and embedding model, filter, nearest neighbours, hybrid + rerank, threshold. Numbered sources go into the prompt; the application turns [n] into the full reference. Common mistake: “Token IDs already capture meaning.” IDs are dictionary positions; the embedding vector carries the meaning.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) gives a language model an open book. Once, offline, every trusted document is extracted, cleaned, cut into chunks, turned into tokens and then into an embedding vector, and stored with its text and metadata in a vector database. Then, for every question, the question is embedded the same way, the nearest chunks are found, filtered, reranked and placed in the prompt with their sources, and the model answers from them and cites them.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: RAG is the whole process: a search step finds excerpts and references, and a language model such as Qwen reads them and writes the answer. Fine-tuning is optional; it can help Qwen read heritage evidence more faithfully. A model only knows its training data, can invent fluent answers, cannot show where a fact came from, and must be retrained to learn anything new. RAG fixes all four: your own documents, grounded answers, a source for every claim, and updates by re-indexing a document. Both student projects depend on it.

entries.text: Qwen3.8 8B Qwen3.8 27B 8.2 billion parameters 9.3 GB to train with QLoRA (rank 16) 5.8 GB to answer questions (4-bit) 16 GB Free cloud GPU (T4) ✓ 24 GB RTX 3090 / 4090 ✓ 48 GB Workstation GPU ✓ 80 GB Data-centre GPU ✓ 8B trains on a free 16 GB T4 (Kaggle or Colab). Because RAG supplies the facts, a smaller fine-tuned model often answers as accurately as a larger one: compare both on the same test questions before paying for the larger GPU. Part 7 : QLoRA

entries.heading: Two projects, one recipe
entries.text: open-weight Qwen + RAG (facts) + fine-tuning (voice) + vision (if photos) TurathAI: question → RAG (stories) → fine-tuned Qwen → story with its source. UTAS-70: photo → YOLO → name → RAG (flora) → fine-tuned Qwen → answer with pages. Pilot on 8B (free 16 GB GPU); train 27B only on a 24 GB+ GPU. Common mistake: “Fine-tuning will teach the model all the facts.” Facts and references live in RAG; fine-tuning teaches how to answer.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: Both student projects teach a free, open-weight foundation model (Qwen3.8 8B or 27B) to be an expert: TurathAI in Omani intangible heritage, UTAS-70 in recognising Omani plants. Both use RAG, the key component, for verified facts and their references, and fine-tuning for the expert way of answering. UTAS-70 adds computer vision in front: YOLO recognises the plant first, and its name opens the RAG archive.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: Seeing the shared recipe first makes both projects easier to follow and shows students how to plan their own: decide where the facts live (RAG), what the model must learn to do (fine-tuning), and whether the input needs to be recognised first (vision).

entries.heading: TurathAI: fine-tuning a model on Omani heritage
entries.text: How would you plan a real fine-tuning project from start to finish? Qwen3.8-27B · QLoRA · Unsloth UTAS 2020 TurathAI is a student project at the University of Technology and Applied Sciences (IT Department, College of Computing and Information Sciences), supervised by Dr. Nasser Mohammed Tabook. Its goal: an AI assistant that preserves Omani intangible heritage (folktales, proverbs, customs and traditions) and answers questions about it with references to the original sources. This is the team’s research plan. The steps below follow their report; their measured results will come after implementation.

entries.text: Q1 Does fine-tuning on verified Omani heritage make Qwen3.8-27B more accurate and culturally relevant than the original? Q2 Can the assistant find the right passages in the heritage archive and cite its sources? Q3 Can users study heritage easily, and admins manage the content, in the web app? Q4 Can QLoRA adapt a 27-billion-weight model on limited, rented GPU resources?

entries.heading: The big picture: building the Omani heritage AI assistant
entries.text: Project objective Build a web application that helps users explore Omani oral histories, folktales, proverbs, customs and cultural practices. It combines a fine-tuned Qwen model with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), so it gives clear answers with citations to the original sources. Enlarge Project illustration: the six panels follow the build order, and the bottom row shows what happens each time a user asks a question.

entries.heading: Project workflow: click a step to find it in the illustration
entries.text: 1 Collect and prepare heritage sources College students gather PDFs, text files, Word documents, audio recordings and videos. They extract text from documents, transcribe recordings, and preserve source details such as titles, page numbers and timestamps. In the illustration: Panels 1–2 2 Fine-tune the Qwen model on RunPod Use an open-weight Qwen model in the 27-billion-parameter class as the foundation. Turn about 10–20% of the prepared material into curated JSONL training examples. They teach the model the desired writing style, Omani heritage terminology, and how to explain differences between accounts. In the illustration: Panel 3 3 Build the RAG knowledge base Upload the remaining 80–90% of the material to the retrieval pipeline. Split the text into passages (chunks), turn each passage into an embedding, and store them in a vector database together with their source references. In the illustration: Panel 4 4 Connect both parts in a web application When a user asks a question, RAG retrieves the relevant passages and their sources. The app sends the question, the passages and the source references to the fine-tuned model, which writes the answer. The app shows the answer with its citations. In the illustration: Panels 5–6 and the bottom row

entries.heading: How the source material is divided
entries.text: 10–20% Fine-tuning 80–90% RAG knowledge base Fine-tuning teaches how to answer A small, carefully written set of examples is enough to change behaviour: Arabic style, heritage terms, and comparing accounts fairly. Changing it means training again. RAG supplies what to say, and where it came from Most of the material stays as searchable passages with their references, so facts can be checked and cited. Adding a new verified source needs no retraining.

entries.heading: Follow one question through the application
entries.text: User question RAG retrieves passages + sources Fine-tuned model writes Answer + citations Play When is the Omani khanjar worn, and what is it made of? A student types a question in the web app. Nothing has been searched yet, and the model has not seen this question before. Model selection note The illustration says “Qwen base model”. This plan names Qwen3.8-27B; the exact checkpoint name, revision and licence must be confirmed before setup (phase 1 of the checklist below). Good practice for this design Store the title, page or timestamp with every passage: citations can only be as good as these references. Keep the test questions out of the training examples, splitting by story family, so the evaluation is fair. The 10–20% / 80–90% split describes where the effort goes. Sources behind the training examples can also be indexed, so their facts can be cited too. Get the narrators’ consent for oral recordings, and record the rights for each source in the source register. Watch it happen

entries.heading: Will a 27-billion-weight model fit?
entries.text: QLoRA: 4-bit base + adapters ≈ 23 GB LoRA: 16-bit base + adapters ≈ 61 GB Full fine-tuning: every weight ≈ 201 GB 24 GB 48 GB 80 GB Our classroom estimate for 27B with r = 16 on every layer. A 24 GB card is borderline; 48 GB leaves room for longer Arabic texts. Unsloth’s guide for Qwen3.8-27B: QLoRA works with 24 GB, LoRA needs more than 36 GB, and full fine-tuning about four times more. unsloth.ai That is why TurathAI rents a RunPod GPU and runs a short pilot (Phase 4) before paying for the full training run.

entries.heading: Their training code with Unsloth
entries.text: Copy from unsloth import FastModel # 1) Load the 27B base in 4-bit: it is frozen from here on (QLoRA) # The project names "Qwen3.8-27B". Before a real run, use the exact model ID # and revision from Unsloth's list of supported models, and check its licence. model, tokenizer = FastModel.from_pretrained( model_name = "unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-unsloth-bnb-4bit", max_seq_length = 2048, load_in_4bit = True, full_finetuning = False, ) # 2) Attach LoRA adapters to the language layers only (TurathAI is text-only) model = FastModel.get_peft_model( model, finetune_vision_layers = False, finetune_language_layers = True, finetune_attention_modules = True, finetune_mlp_modules = True, r = 16, lora_alpha = 16, lora_dropout = 0, bias = "none", use_gradient_checkpointing = "unsloth", random_state = 3407, ) # 3) The verified Arabic question-answer pairs, already split by story family from datasets import load_dataset data = load_dataset("json", data_files = { "train": "turath_train.jsonl", "validation": "turath_validation.jsonl"}) def to_chat(row): messages = [{"role": "user", "content": row["question"]}, {"role": "assistant", "content": row["answer"]}] return {"text": tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize = False)} data = data.map(to_chat) # 4) Train on a rented RunPod GPU from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig trainer = SFTTrainer( model = model, tokenizer = tokenizer, train_dataset = data["train"], eval_dataset = data["validation"], args = SFTConfig( dataset_text_field = "text", per_device_train_batch_size = 1, gradient_accumulation_steps = 4, num_train_epochs = 2, learning_rate = 2e-4, optim = "adamw_8bit", logging_steps = 10, output_dir = "turath_outputs", ), ) trainer.train() # 5) Save the adapter: the Phase 5 deliverable (test that it reloads!) model.save_pretrained("turath_lora") tokenizer.save_pretrained("turath_lora") Based on Unsloth’s Qwen3.8-27B guide. Qwen3.8-27B can also read images, so the vision layers are left untouched. Check the official notebook for your library versions before running.

The online part works exactly like the RAG application in part 11: an admin uploads verified records, they are embedded into the vector database, and each question is answered from the retrieved passages with their sources — no retraining needed. entries.heading: Plan your own project: the eight phases
entries.text: 0 / 8 1 Confirm requirements Agreed scope, permissions, the exact Qwen checkpoint and its licence, and success criteria, with the supervisor. 2 Collect and verify A source register (title, region, rights, verification) and reviewed Arabic text, with story variants kept. 3 Prepare the datasets train.jsonl, validation.jsonl and test.jsonl, split by source or story family so no story leaks into the test. 4 Baseline and GPU pilot The original model’s answers to the test questions, plus a short RunPod pilot: chat template, memory, batch size, adapter save and reload. 5 Fine-tune The LoRA adapter files and a training log: loss, GPU memory, time and the full configuration. 6 Evaluate Scoring sheets for both models on the same unseen questions, with the same generation settings. 7 Integrate The web app: a User Dashboard and an Admin Dashboard, connected to the model and to retrieval with citations. 8 Document Results, limitations, deployment steps and the controlled process for adding new verified heritage.

entries.heading: Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: How is a vision model fine-tuned? frozen body + new head Fine-tuning is not only for language models. A CNN trained on ImageNet already knows edges, textures and shapes. Freeze that body, replace its 1,000-class head with one output per species, train the head, then gently unfreeze the top blocks. This is called transfer learning. Watch it happen

entries.heading: Transfer learning: fine-tuning a CNN on Dhofar plants
entries.text: convolutional body (the backbone) old head lr = 0.001 a photo augmented copies (training only) (pixel ÷ 255 − mean) ÷ std edges, colours textures shapes plant parts whole plants tabby cat school bus daisy pizza 1,000 classes this head will be removed Click any part of the picture, or a name here, for a full explanation: The photo Early blocks: general features Top blocks: specific features The head 1 / 7 A CNN already trained on ImageNet Start from a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on ImageNet: about 1.2 million photos in 1,000 everyday classes. Its early layers learned edges and colours, the middle layers textures and shapes, and the late layers whole parts such as leaves, petals and bark. Play

entries.heading: Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: How is a vision model fine-tuned? frozen body + new head Try it. Play the scene and watch where the gradient stops in stages 1 and 2. Then find the share of numbers trained with MobileNetV2 and 6 species, switch the split to “by tree”, and raise the threshold until the unknown plant is refused.

entries.heading: Two kinds of fine-tuning, one idea
entries.text: UTAS-70 fine-tunes two different models. Both keep what a big pre-trained model already knows, freeze most of it, and train a small new part on the project’s own data. The CNN (sees the photo) The language model (writes the answer) Starts from A CNN pre-trained on ImageNet (MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B0, ResNet50) An open-weight language model (Qwen3.8-27B) What stays frozen The convolutional body (all of it in stage 1, the lower blocks in stage 2) Every weight of the base model, stored in 4-bit What is trained A new head (one output per species), then the top blocks Small LoRA adapters A and B added beside the frozen matrices Share of numbers trained Head only: well under 1% of the network Usually around 0.5–2% of the model Training data Labelled photos: one folder per species, 100–150+ photos each JSONL lines: instruction → response, written from the sources Loss Cross-entropy over the species classes Cross-entropy over the next token of the answer Typical learning rate About 1e-3 for the head, then about 1e-5 for the unfrozen blocks About 2e-4 for the LoRA adapters Output One species and a confidence (a probability) A written answer, token by token How it is judged Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix Factual accuracy, relevance, hallucination, consistency, judged by people Hardware A free 16 GB cloud GPU is plenty A 27B model in 4-bit needs about 24 GB Same recipe: a general model + a frozen body + a small trained part + your labelled data. The new head of a CNN plays the role that the LoRA adapter plays in a language model.

entries.heading: Pick a backbone: how much do you actually train?
entries.text: MobileNetV2 EfficientNet-B0 ResNet50 Species (classes) 6 Stage 1: head only Everything (from scratch-like) Frozen body 2,223,872 New head 1,280 × 6 + 6 = 7,686 Trained numbers 7,686 ( 0.34% ) File ≈ 9 MB ImageNet top-1 71.9 % 0.3 GFLOPs Smallest and fastest; built for phones. Compare with LoRA in part 5: there 1–2% of the numbers train. Here, with a frozen backbone, it is even less, which is why a free GPU and a few hundred photos per species are enough.

entries.heading: Prepare a photo: resize, normalize, augment
entries.text: 224 × 224 × 3 Rotate 0 ° Zoom × 1.00 Brightness × 1.00 Flip left–right Normalize one leaf pixel R G B pixel 86 140 62 ÷ 255 0.337 0.549 0.243 − mean 0.485 0.456 0.406 ÷ std 0.229 0.224 0.225 = -0.65 0.42 -0.72 New random batch Every epoch sees a slightly different version of each photo, so the model learns the plant, not one picture of it. Only the training set is augmented: validation and test photos stay real, or the score would describe made-up photos.

entries.heading: Split by tree, not by photo
entries.text: Random photos (wrong) By tree / observation (right) Tree A train train validation train Tree B train train train test Tree C train test train train Tree D validation train train train Tree E train train test train Tree F test train validation train 4 trees have photos in both training and test Test accuracy looks like 97%, but the model has already seen these trees from almost the same angle. It measures memory. The same rule as splitting JSONL by source or story family in part 3: anything nearly identical must stay on one side. (The scores here are illustrations.)

entries.heading: Read a confusion matrix
entries.text: Rows are the real species, columns what the model said. The diagonal is right; everything else is a mistake, and it tells you which mistake. (Illustrative test of 120 photos.) real ↓ / said → Frankincense tree Myrrh Baobab Desert rose Frankincense tree 26 3 0 1 Myrrh 5 22 1 2 Baobab 0 1 28 1 Desert rose 1 1 0 28 Myrrh Precision 81.5% of the 27 photos it called “Myrrh”, 22 really were Recall 73.3% of the 30 real ones, it found 22 F1 77.2% the balance of the two Accuracy (all) 86.7% Macro F1 (mean of species) 86.6% The biggest mistake is myrrh called frankincense: both are Burseraceae with similar bark. The fix is data, not settings: more photos of the parts that differ (leaves, flowers, fruit). Macro F1 gives each species the same weight, so a rare species cannot hide behind a common one.

entries.heading: Set the confidence threshold
entries.text: Answer only when confidence ≥ 70 % Frankincense tree said : Frankincense tree · 97 % Baobab said : Baobab · 94 % Desert rose said : Desert rose · 91 % Dhofar aloe said : Dhofar aloe · 88 % unknown plant said : Dhofar aloe · 83 % Myrrh said : Myrrh · 79 % Sycamore fig said : Sycamore fig · 74 % Myrrh said : Frankincense tree · 66 % Frankincense tree said : Frankincense tree · 61 % unknown plant said : Desert rose · 55 % Desert rose said : Myrrh · 47 % unknown plant said : Sycamore fig · 38 % 6 right answers shown 1 wrong answers shown 1 good photos refused 2 / 3 unknown plants rejected Raising the threshold removes wrong answers but refuses more good photos. Look at the unknown plant at 83%: softmax must choose one of the known species, so a confident answer can still be about a plant the model has never seen. Choose the threshold on validation data and check it on an out-of-scope set.

entries.heading: Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: How is a vision model fine-tuned? frozen body + new head 15

entries.heading: Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: frozen CNN body + new head (1 output per species) Transfer learning: start from ImageNet weights, replace the head, train it; then unfreeze the top blocks at about 1/100 of the learning rate. 224 × 224, ImageNet normalization; augment the training set only, after a split by tree or observation. Report precision, recall, macro F1 and the confusion matrix; set the threshold on validation data. Common mistake: “A confident prediction means a known plant.” Softmax always picks a known class; test with out-of-scope photos.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: Fine-tuning is not only for language models. A CNN trained on ImageNet already knows edges, textures and shapes. Freeze that body, replace its 1,000-class head with one output per species, train the head, then gently unfreeze the top blocks. This is called transfer learning.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: A few hundred photos per species are far too few to train millions of numbers from zero, but enough to train a small head on top of features that already work. It is the same reason LoRA works: keep the general knowledge, train a small new part.

entries.heading: Real project: UTAS-70
entries.text: YOLO + RAG + fine-tuning: how do eyes, memory and brain join? YOLO + RAG archive + QLoRA UTAS-70 is a final-year student project: a bilingual assistant for the native plants of Dhofar, built from three parts. The eyes: a fine-tuned YOLO model names the plant in a photo. The memory: a RAG digital archive holds all the references, and the name finds the right passages. The brain: Qwen3.8-27B, fine-tuned with QLoRA on examples from about 20% of the references, writes the answer in a botanist’s style. The relay: YOLO → RAG → fine-tuned model The whole system 1 YOLO sees 2 RAG archive remembers 3 Fine-tuned Qwen speaks photo Boswellia sacra · 89% 2 passages + sources final answer confidence threshold 70% — Definition YOLO (“You Only Look Once”) is a computer-vision model that looks at the whole photo in a single pass and answers two questions at once: what is in it, and where. a photo a name, a box, a confidence 1 / 12

entries.heading: What is YOLO?
entries.text: The photo arrives. YOLO scans it once, all of it, instead of sliding a window over it many times. That single look is why it is fast enough for a phone. Play

entries.heading: Real project: UTAS-70
entries.text: YOLO + RAG + fine-tuning: how do eyes, memory and brain join? YOLO + RAG archive + QLoRA Try it. Follow the photo through the scene. Then switch off each of the three parts to see what breaks, untick “keep every reference in the archive”, and search the archive for the flowering season without the name filter.

entries.heading: The project on one page
entries.text: Problem Knowledge about Dhofar’s native plants is spread over botanical books and studies, and general chatbots and plant apps know little about them. Idea Three parts: YOLO names the plant in the photo (eyes), the name searches a RAG digital archive of all the references (memory), and a QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen writes a sourced answer in Arabic or English (brain). Scope Phase 1 is a proof of concept: a selected set of Dhofar species. Phase 2 adds other regions of Oman by repeating the data steps, without changing the code.

entries.heading: Every research question has a hypothesis and a test
entries.text: RQ1 RQ2 RQ3 RQ4 RQ1 Does a QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen answer Dhofar plant questions more accurately, with fewer hallucinations, than the same base model? Hypothesis H1: the fine-tuned model is more accurate, relevant and consistent. Test About 100 held-out questions, asked to the base model, the fine-tuned model, and the fine-tuned model with RAG. Part 7 : QLoRA

entries.heading: Three parts, one assistant
entries.text: Each part does one job and learns from different data. Vision recognises, the archive remembers, the fine-tuned model knows how to answer. Eyes · computer vision YOLO Finds the plant in the photo and names its species, with a confidence. switched on Memory · RAG digital archive RAG Keeps every reference (books, papers, field notes, herbarium sheets) as tagged, searchable passages, and returns the ones about this plant and this question. switched on Brain · fine-tuned Qwen Qwen3.8-27B + LoRA Reads the passages and the question and writes the answer the way a Dhofar botanist would: names, description, place, uses, cautions, source. switched on Memory · RAG digital archive Built from Nothing is trained. Documents are scanned, cleaned, cut into passages, tagged (species, names, place, topic, source, page) and indexed. Adding a book needs no retraining. In → out The species name + the question → The top passages, each with its source and page How to test it Retrieval hit rate: for test questions, is the passage holding the answer in the top 3? scan / PDF OCR (ar + en) clean cut into passages tag: species, place, topic, source, page embed (multilingual) index Use an embedding model that understands Arabic and English (for example BGE-M3) and a vector index such as FAISS or Chroma. Search in two steps: filter by the species name from YOLO, then rank by meaning. Part 12 : RAG in depth The hiker asks, in Arabic: “What is this plant used for?” Frankincense tree (Boswellia sacra). Its resin is tapped from the bark and burned as incense; it is also used in traditional practices. (Source C, p. __; Field notes 3) For education only. ✓ right plant ✓ every fact sourced ✓ house style

entries.heading: Share the references: style vs facts
entries.text: References used to write fine-tuning examples 20 % Keep every reference in the RAG archive too (recommended) FT RAG FT RAG FT RAG FT RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG RAG Flora books Research papers Field notes Herbarium sheets 4 / 20 teach the style (fine-tuning) 20 / 20 give the facts (RAG archive) 0 facts only in the weights: no source, cannot be updated A good balance: a varied slice (books, papers, field notes, herbarium sheets) teaches the answer style; the archive holds everything, so every fact has a source. Write some test questions from references that were not used for fine-tuning. If the system answers those well too, the facts are really coming from RAG, not from memory.

entries.heading: Search the digital archive
entries.text: Name from YOLO Frankincense tree Myrrh Desert rose Question What is it used for? Where does it grow in Dhofar? What does it look like? When does it flower? Filter by the species name first 0.79 The resin is tapped from the bark and burned as incense; it is also used in traditional practices. Boswellia sacra · Source C, p. __ 0.71 Harvesters cut the bark and collect the dried resin some weeks later. Boswellia sacra · Field notes 3 Every passage is about the frankincense tree. The model answers from these and cites them. What one archived passage looks like { "id" : " p2 " , "species" : " Boswellia sacra " , "topic" : " uses " , "source" : " Source C, p. __ " , "text" : " The resin is tapped from the bark and burned as incense; it is also used in traditional practices. " } The passages and similarity numbers are illustrations. In the real archive, the species tag comes from the same scientific name used as the YOLO class name.

entries.heading: Four layers, each with one job
entries.text: 1 · Presentation Web interface (Gradio / FastAPI) 2 · Application Integration module in Photo, question, classifier result out The prompt for the model and the final reply The conductor: checks the threshold, sends the name to the archive, builds the prompt, remembers the species, handles errors. 3 · AI models YOLO (eyes) + fine-tuned Qwen (brain) 4 · Knowledge (memory) RAG digital archive: tagged passages, vector index, name index Clear inputs and outputs let three students build the layers in parallel and test each alone. Species, paths and model names live in configuration files, so Phase 2 adds data, not code.
