entries.text: Boswellia sacra Family Burseraceae Arabic and local names Luban (اللبان) Description A small tree with papery, peeling bark; its resin oozes from cuts in the bark. Habitat Dry slopes and plains, mostly beyond the reach of the monsoon mist. Season — not in the sources Uses Its resin is burned as incense and used in traditional practices. Every fact: source and page. Illustrative record. question → answer question + record → answer English العربية { "instruction" : " Where does the frankincense tree grow in Dhofar? " , "context" : " Family: Burseraceae | Arabic and local names: Luban (اللبان) | Description: A small tree with papery, peeling bark; its resin oozes from cuts in the bark. | Habitat: Dry slopes and plains, mostly beyond the reach of the monsoon mist. | Uses: Its resin is burned as incense and used in traditional practices. " , "response" : " In Dhofar it grows on dry slopes and plains, mostly beyond the reach of the monsoon mist. " , "species" : " Boswellia sacra " , "source" : " Source A, p. __ " } Same shape as at answer time: the model learns to read the record and answer from it. Reviewed against the source: add to train.jsonl

entries.heading: Compare three systems on the same question
entries.text: Where does the frankincense tree grow in Dhofar? Base Qwen, no fine-tuning Frankincense grows across the Arabian Peninsula and the Horn of Africa, often in sandy deserts and coastal areas. Accuracy ● ○ Relevance ● ○ Traceable ○○ General and partly wrong for Dhofar; no source. Fine-tuned UTAS-70 In Dhofar, the frankincense tree grows on dry slopes and plains, mostly away from the monsoon mist. Accuracy ●● Relevance ●● Traceable ● ○ The right facts and tone, but it cannot show where they came from. Ask the next system Consistency: the same question, three wordings Where does the frankincense tree grow in Dhofar? In which parts of Dhofar is Boswellia sacra found? أين تنمو شجرة اللبان في ظفار؟ A consistent model gives the same facts all three times, in either language. Only the three-way comparison shows what each part adds: fine-tuning improves how it answers; the record makes the answer true and traceable. The answers and marks here are illustrations.

entries.heading: A guide for your own project
entries.text: Twelve habits from this project that apply to any fine-tuning project. Tick the ones your plan already has. 0 / 12 Fix the targets before the data Write the species list, the target scores and the test plan in step 1. Each research question should already have its test. Part 10 : Workflow and evaluation One key joins everything Use the scientific name as the YOLO class name and as the species tag on every archive passage. Then a prediction finds its passages with no guessing. Part 3 : From documents to JSONL No fact from memory Every fact carries its source and page; an empty field stays empty. The model can only be as true as its data. Part 3 : From documents to JSONL Train in the shape you will use At answer time the model receives the retrieved passages as context. So include them in the training lines too (question + passages → answer), not only question → answer, and add lines where the passages lack the answer. Part 11 : Fine-tuning, RAG, or both? Facts in the archive, style in the weights Fine-tune on a slice of the references to teach how to answer; keep every reference, that slice included, in the RAG archive. Then every fact can be cited and updated without retraining. Part 11 : Fine-tuning, RAG, or both? Split by group, then augment Photos of the same tree, day or photographer stay in one split, and only the training set is augmented. Otherwise the test score is too good to be true. Part 15 : Fine-tuning for images A threshold is not a detector Softmax always picks one of the known species, even for a plant it has never seen. Keep an out-of-scope test set and report how many unknown plants are correctly rejected. Part 15 : Fine-tuning for images Check that the GPU really fits Add up base weights, adapters and working memory before planning on a free GPU. Pilot on a small Qwen first, then train the large one on a GPU that fits. Part 7 : QLoRA QLoRA memory, rank 16 (rough classroom estimate) Qwen 4B 5.8 GB 16 GB ✓ 24 GB ✓ Qwen 8B 9.3 GB 16 GB ✓ 24 GB ✓ Qwen 27B 23.3 GB 16 GB ✕ 24 GB ✓ A free Kaggle or Colab T4 has 16 GB: enough for a pilot on a small Qwen, not for 27B. Plan the 27B run on a 24 GB GPU or larger. Compare three systems, not two Base model, fine-tuned model, and fine-tuned model with RAG, on the same unseen questions. Only then can you say what each part adds. Part 10 : Workflow and evaluation Name things the same everywhere Use the same model name, version and settings in the review, the method, the code and the results, so a reader can rerun exactly what you did. Part 10 : Workflow and evaluation Safety is part of the design A plant assistant must say it is for education, not for medicinal or safety decisions, and refuse to guess about edibility or treatment. Leave it rerunnable Fixed seeds, saved settings, licences for every photo, and species, paths and models in configuration files, so Phase 2 adds data, not code.

entries.heading: The idea
entries.text: UTAS-70 is a final-year student project: a bilingual assistant for the native plants of Dhofar, built from three parts. The eyes: a fine-tuned YOLO model names the plant in a photo. The memory: a RAG digital archive holds all the references, and the name finds the right passages. The brain: Qwen3.8-27B, fine-tuned with QLoRA on examples from about 20% of the references, writes the answer in a botanist’s style.

entries.heading: Why it matters
entries.text: It joins almost everything in this lab: data from books (part 3), QLoRA and Unsloth (parts 7–8), evaluation (part 10), retrieval (part 11) and vision fine-tuning (part 13). Use it as a template for planning your own project.

entries.heading: Teach a ready-made model your own subject
entries.text: Sixteen short parts in six chapters, in the order a real project follows: from the base model and its data, through LoRA, quantization, QLoRA and Unsloth, to training, evaluation and RAG in depth, and then two real student projects that share one recipe, one of them with computer vision. Each part has an animation to watch, tools to try and a card to remember. Search the lab Ctrl K Reference sheet Review

entries.heading: Reference sheet: fine-tuning on one page
entries.text: The summary card of every part, grouped by chapter, and the glossary. Print it, or keep it open while you work. Print or save as PDF

entries.heading: 1Foundations the base model
entries.title: 1 Foundations the base model

entries.heading: Why fine-tune
entries.text: Open the part base model + your examples → specialist Fine-tuning continues the training of a model that already knows language, on your own examples. It teaches a subject, a format or a way of answering; it starts from open weights, not from zero. It is not always needed: try prompting first, and use RAG for new facts. Common mistake: “You must fine-tune to add knowledge.” New facts and documents usually belong in RAG. 2

entries.heading: Key words
entries.text: Open the part z = x₁w₁ + x₂w₂ + b Parameters are learned numbers: weights (w) and biases (b). Training is one loop: forward → loss → gradient → update → next batch. Frozen means not updated. It does not mean inactive. Common mistake: “The model stores facts in its parameters like a file.” Knowledge is a pattern spread over many numbers.

entries.heading: 2Data the examples
entries.title: 2 Data the examples

entries.heading: From documents to JSONL
entries.text: Open the part document → text → pairs → JSONL → tokens JSONL: one complete JSON object per line, in UTF-8. Split by source (about 80 / 10 / 10), never by random lines. Mask the prompt and train on the answer; check max_seq_length does not cut answers. Common mistake: “Valid JSONL means good data.” JSONL is only a format; truth needs expert review.

entries.heading: 3Methods LoRA · 4-bit · QLoRA
entries.title: 3 Methods LoRA · 4-bit · QLoRA

entries.heading: Four ways to fine-tune
entries.text: Open the part full · partial · LoRA · QLoRA Full fine-tuning updates every weight; partial updates chosen layers. LoRA freezes the base and trains small added matrices A and B. QLoRA is LoRA on a base stored in 4-bit. Common mistake: “Quantization removes weights.” That is pruning. Quantization keeps every weight with fewer bits. 5

entries.heading: LoRA
entries.text: Open the part y = W·x + (α/r)·B(A·x) A is r × in, B is out × r: 1,000 × 1,000 at r = 8 trains 16,000 numbers (1.6%). A starts random, B starts at zero, so training starts exactly from the base model. After training, merge once: W′ = W + s·B·A, or keep the adapter as a small file. Common mistake: “LoRA means a low number of adapters.” It means Low-Rank Adaptation. 6

entries.heading: Quantization
entries.text: Open the part memory = parameters × bits ÷ 8 4 bits name only 16 levels; each weight is rounded to the nearest one. NF4 packs its levels near zero, where most weights are. One scale (absmax) is stored per block of 64 weights. Common mistake: “Fewer bits means fewer weights.” The count stays the same; each weight just takes less memory. 7

entries.heading: QLoRA
entries.text: Open the part 4-bit frozen base + 16-bit LoRA adapters Order: load the base in 4-bit, freeze it, attach adapters, train. Stored in 4-bit, calculated in 16-bit (bfloat16). 27B: 54 GB at 16-bit, 13.5 GB at 4-bit for the raw weights, which is not a full GPU budget. Common mistake: “QLoRA compresses the model after training.” The base is already 4-bit during training.

entries.heading: 4Training Unsloth · the loop
entries.title: 4 Training Unsloth · the loop

entries.heading: Unsloth
entries.text: Open the part from_pretrained(load_in_4bit) → get_peft_model(r) → train → save Unsloth is software that runs LoRA and QLoRA faster and with less memory. It works with PyTorch, a trainer (TRL) and the GPU; you still choose data, model and settings. Export the adapter alone, a merged 16-bit model, or a 4-bit GGUF file. Common mistake: “Unsloth is a different training method.” It is a toolkit that implements LoRA and QLoRA. 9

entries.heading: One training step
entries.text: Open the part loss = −log p(correct token) One step: forward → loss → backward → optimizer update, on one batch. Effective batch = batch × accumulation × GPUs (2 × 8 × 1 = 16). Too large a learning rate diverges; rising validation loss means overfitting. Common mistake: “Lower training loss means better answers.” Only unseen test questions show that.

entries.heading: 5Evaluate and deploy test · RAG · RAG in depth
entries.title: 5 Evaluate and deploy test · RAG · RAG in depth

entries.heading: Workflow and evaluation
entries.text: Open the part baseline → data → configure → pilot → train → evaluate → deploy Record the base model’s answers first, so there is something to compare with. Compare base and adapter on the same unseen questions; let an expert judge. An adapter needs its exact base model; re-evaluate after merging or quantizing. Common mistake: “If training runs, the model is good.” Running proves execution, not quality. 11

entries.heading: Fine-tuning, RAG, or both?
entries.text: Open the part RAG = the library · fine-tuning = the storyteller All real stories go into RAG; 5–20% curated teaching examples go into fine-tuning. Write training examples as question + retrieved context → answer with the source. Vector search finds by meaning; when nothing matches, the model should say so. Common mistake: “Put the same stories in both.” The model then mixes memorized and retrieved versions. 12

entries.heading: RAG in depth
entries.text: Open the part documents → chunks → tokens → vectors → search → cited answer Indexing runs once: extract, clean, chunk (200–500 tokens, 10–20% overlap), embed, store vector + text + metadata. Answering runs per question: same tokenizer and embedding model, filter, nearest neighbours, hybrid + rerank, threshold. Numbered sources go into the prompt; the application turns [n] into the full reference. Common mistake: “Token IDs already capture meaning.” IDs are dictionary positions; the embedding vector carries the meaning.

entries.heading: 6Real projects one recipe · TurathAI · vision · UTAS-70
entries.title: 6 Real projects one recipe · TurathAI · vision · UTAS-70

entries.heading: Two projects, one recipe
entries.text: Open the part open-weight Qwen + RAG (facts) + fine-tuning (voice) + vision (if photos) TurathAI: question → RAG (stories) → fine-tuned Qwen → story with its source. UTAS-70: photo → YOLO → name → RAG (flora) → fine-tuned Qwen → answer with pages. Pilot on 8B (free 16 GB GPU); train 27B only on a 24 GB+ GPU. Common mistake: “Fine-tuning will teach the model all the facts.” Facts and references live in RAG; fine-tuning teaches how to answer. 14

entries.heading: Real project: TurathAI
entries.text: Open the part verified heritage + QLoRA + RAG with citations Verified, credited sources; split by story family so the test is truly unseen. QLoRA with Unsloth on a rented GPU, after a short pilot run. Judge faithfulness, cultural tone and honest “not found” answers. Common mistake: “The model should memorize every story.” The archive stays in RAG; the model learns to tell and cite. 15

entries.heading: Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: Open the part frozen CNN body + new head (1 output per species) Transfer learning: start from ImageNet weights, replace the head, train it; then unfreeze the top blocks at about 1/100 of the learning rate. 224 × 224, ImageNet normalization; augment the training set only, after a split by tree or observation. Report precision, recall, macro F1 and the confusion matrix; set the threshold on validation data. Common mistake: “A confident prediction means a known plant.” Softmax always picks a known class; test with out-of-scope photos. 16

entries.heading: Real project: UTAS-70
entries.text: Open the part YOLO (eyes) → RAG archive (memory) → fine-tuned Qwen (brain) YOLO names the plant; the name filters the archive search; the model writes from the passages. About 20% of the references teach the style (fine-tuning); the archive keeps 100% for the facts. One key, the scientific name, is the YOLO class name and the species tag on every passage. Common mistake: “Fine-tune on some references, put only the rest in RAG.” Keep every reference in the archive; fine-tuning teaches how to answer, not what.

entries.heading: Parameter (weight) part 2 · Key words
entries.text: A learned number inside the model or the adapter. There are two kinds: weights (w), which set how strongly each input counts, and biases (b), extra numbers added before the activation function. A “27B” model holds 27 billion such numbers: numbers, not facts or documents. Knowledge is spread across many of them.

entries.heading: Frozen parameter part 4 · Four ways to fine-tune
entries.text: A parameter that training is told not to change. It still takes part in every calculation: frozen means not updated, not inactive.

entries.heading: Trainable parameter part 5 · LoRA
entries.text: A parameter the optimizer is allowed to change. In LoRA these are only the numbers in the small matrices A and B: the adapter.

entries.heading: Activation (forward pass) part 9 · One training step
entries.text: An in-between value computed for the current input as it passes through the layers. The frozen layers and the adapters both compute activations.

entries.heading: Loss part 9 · One training step
entries.text: One number that says how far the model’s predicted next tokens are from the target answer. Lower is a better fit to the training examples.

entries.heading: Gradient (backward pass) part 9 · One training step
entries.text: A signal for each trainable number: which way, and how strongly, a small change would lower the loss. It travels back through the frozen layers to reach the adapters, but the frozen layers keep no gradient of their own.

entries.heading: Optimizer (update) part 9 · One training step
entries.text: The algorithm, for example AdamW, that uses the gradients to change the trainable numbers a little. The learning rate sets how big each change is.

entries.heading: Batch, step and epoch part 9 · One training step
entries.text: A batch is the group of examples handled together; one step is one update after a batch; an epoch is one full pass through the training data. Then it all repeats.

entries.heading: Transfer learning part 15 · Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: Starting from a model trained on a large general task and fine-tuning it for yours, instead of training from zero.

entries.heading: CNN (convolutional neural network) part 15 · Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: A network for images. Small filters slide over the picture; early layers find edges, later layers whole shapes.

entries.heading: Backbone and head part 15 · Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: The backbone turns a photo into features; the head is the last layer that turns features into one score per class.

entries.heading: Data augmentation part 15 · Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: Making changed copies of training photos (turned, flipped, zoomed, brighter) so the model learns the plant, not one picture.

entries.heading: Precision, recall and F1 part 15 · Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: Precision: of what it called X, how much was X. Recall: of all real X, how much it found. F1 balances the two; macro F1 averages it over classes.

entries.heading: Confusion matrix part 15 · Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: A table of real class (rows) against predicted class (columns). The diagonal is right; the other cells show which mistakes happen.

entries.heading: Confidence threshold part 15 · Fine-tuning for images
entries.text: The lowest probability at which the system accepts a prediction; below it, it asks for a better photo.

entries.heading: Digital archive (RAG) part 16 · Real project: UTAS-70
entries.text: All the references cut into passages, each tagged with species, place, topic, source and page, and indexed so a search finds the right ones.

entries.heading: YOLO part 16 · Real project: UTAS-70
entries.text: A family of fast vision models that can classify a photo or draw a box around each object. Fine-tuned from pretrained weights on your own labelled photos.

entries.heading: Metadata filter part 16 · Real project: UTAS-70
entries.text: Narrowing a search by a tag before ranking by meaning, so only passages about the named plant compete.

entries.heading: Open weight part 1 · Why fine-tune
entries.text: The weights can be downloaded under a licence. It does not mean frozen, and not always free to use for anything: check the licence.

entries.heading: Token and tokenizer part 3 · From documents to JSONL
entries.text: The tokenizer cuts text into pieces called tokens and gives each an ID number. The model only ever sees these numbers.

entries.heading: Chat template part 3 · From documents to JSONL
entries.text: The model’s own markers that show where the user’s turn and the assistant’s turn begin and end. Each model family has its own.

entries.heading: JSONL part 3 · From documents to JSONL
entries.text: A text file with one complete JSON object per line. A storage format, not a teaching method: it guarantees neither truth nor coverage.

entries.heading: SFT part 3 · From documents to JSONL
entries.text: Supervised fine-tuning: training on examples that come with the target answer.

entries.heading: PEFT part 4 · Four ways to fine-tune
entries.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: adapting a model by training relatively few parameters. LoRA is the best-known PEFT method.

entries.heading: RAG part 11 · Fine-tuning, RAG, or both?
entries.text: Retrieval-augmented generation: find relevant source passages at answer time and give them to the model as context. It changes no weights.

entries.heading: Chunk and overlap part 12 · RAG in depth
entries.text: A piece of a document, a few hundred tokens long, that is embedded and retrieved as one unit. Overlap repeats a little text between neighbours so an idea is not cut in half.

entries.heading: Embedding vector part 12 · RAG in depth
entries.text: A list of hundreds of numbers that an embedding model computes for a text. Texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions.

entries.heading: Vector database part 12 · RAG in depth
entries.text: Stores each chunk’s vector, text and metadata, with an index (such as HNSW) that finds the nearest vectors quickly.

entries.heading: Cosine similarity part 12 · RAG in depth
entries.text: How closely two vectors point in the same direction, from −1 to 1. Used to rank chunks against the question.

entries.heading: Hybrid search and reranking part 12 · RAG in depth
entries.text: Combining vector search (meaning) with keyword search such as BM25 (exact words), then letting a reranker read the question with each chunk to choose the best few.

entries.heading: Open book and coach (RAG + fine-tuning) part 11 · Fine-tuning, RAG, or both?
entries.text: RAG is the open book: it looks up approved passages and their sources at answer time, and the collection can grow without retraining. Fine-tuning is the coaching: it teaches how to answer, such as clear Arabic, keeping a proverb’s wording, and showing differing accounts.

entries.heading: The two checks part 11 · Fine-tuning, RAG, or both?
entries.text: Test RAG first, and judge each answer twice. Did it find the right passage? If not, improve the search or the collection. Did it explain it well? If it repeatedly does not, fine-tuning can help.

entries.heading: Fair comparison (base vs fine-tuned) part 12 · RAG in depth
entries.text: Give regular Qwen and fine-tuned Qwen the same held-out questions and the same retrieved passages, then check facts, cited sources, and whether each says when the evidence is insufficient. Only a consistent gain shows that fine-tuning adds accuracy.

entries.heading: Adapter part 5 · LoRA
entries.text: A small trainable part added to an existing model to adapt it. It cannot answer on its own: it needs its matching base model.

entries.heading: LoRA part 5 · LoRA
entries.text: Low-Rank Adaptation: learn a change to a weight matrix written as two thin matrices, ΔW = s × B·A. “Low rank”, not “a low number of adapters”.

entries.heading: Rank r and alpha part 5 · LoRA
entries.text: r is the width of the bottleneck between A and B: more rank, more capacity and more trainable numbers. alpha sets the scale s = alpha ÷ r of the adapter’s effect.

entries.heading: Quantization part 6 · Quantization
entries.text: Storing numbers with fewer bits, usually as an approximation. The number of weights stays the same; each takes less memory.

entries.heading: NF4 part 6 · Quantization
entries.text: “4-bit NormalFloat”: a 4-bit format whose 16 levels are packed near zero, where trained weights usually are. Used by QLoRA.

entries.heading: QLoRA part 7 · QLoRA
entries.text: Train LoRA adapters on top of a frozen base model that is stored in 4-bit during training. Not a compression step after training.

entries.heading: VRAM part 7 · QLoRA
entries.text: The memory on the GPU. The weights, adapters, optimizer state and activations must all fit in it.

entries.heading: Unsloth part 8 · Unsloth
entries.text: A software toolkit that loads supported models, attaches adapters and makes training faster and lighter. It is software, not a method and not a layer.

entries.heading: Learning rate part 9 · One training step
entries.text: How big each optimizer step is. Too small: slow. Too large: the loss jumps around or blows up.

entries.heading: Gradient accumulation part 9 · One training step
entries.text: Add up the gradients of several small batches before one update, to act like a bigger batch without the memory.

entries.heading: Validation set part 10 · Workflow and evaluation
entries.text: Examples kept out of training and used to guide decisions while training, such as when to stop.

entries.heading: Test set part 10 · Workflow and evaluation
entries.text: Examples held back until the very end for the final, honest assessment. Never tune settings on it.

entries.heading: Checkpoint part 10 · Workflow and evaluation
entries.text: A saved snapshot of the training state or of the adapter, so a good earlier version can be recovered.

entries.heading: Merge part 10 · Workflow and evaluation
entries.text: Adding the learned change B·A into W once, so the model has its original shape with the skill built in and no separate adapter.

entries.heading: Teach a ready-made model your own subject
entries.text: Sixteen short parts in six chapters, in the order a real project follows: from the base model and its data, through LoRA, quantization, QLoRA and Unsloth, to training, evaluation and RAG in depth, and then two real student projects that share one recipe, one of them with computer vision. Each part has an animation to watch, tools to try and a card to remember. Search the lab Ctrl K Reference sheet

Lesson 12 of 12 How is knowledge organised so people and AI can use it? Tell a taxonomy, an ontology, a knowledge graph and semantics apart, and build each one for a real example. Hide intro Continue

entries.heading: The ideas
entries.text: A taxonomy groups information into categories and subcategories: what belongs under what. An ontology adds properties, labelled relationships and rules, so a system can explain and conclude. RDF writes each fact as a triple (subject, predicate, object), so facts connect and a reasoning engine can derive new ones. A knowledge graph stores the actual facts as connected triples that follow the ontology. Semantics fixes what each term and link means, so every system reads it the same way.

Knowledge structures

entries.heading: Organise what we know: taxonomy, ontology, knowledge graph and semantics
entries.text: How information is classified, defined, connected and understood, by people and by AI systems. Vectors in RAG find text that sounds similar; these four structures say exactly what things are and how they relate. Eight short parts, with examples from the Omani heritage archive and the Dhofar University academic guide.

entries.heading: What is a taxonomy?
entries.text: A taxonomy is a system for organising information into groups and subgroups, so people can find it, add to it and manage it consistently. A taxonomy groups information into categories and subcategories. We use it to find the right information faster and to describe it consistently. You do not have to build one for every AI project, but when a collection grows, it tells everyone where things belong. In one sentence: a taxonomy tells us where to put new information, and where to look for it later.

entries.heading: Two examples: the Omani heritage archive and the Dhofar University guide
A taxonomy for an Omani heritage AI assistant
entries.text: In an Omani heritage archive, oral traditions can be a main category, with proverbs and folktales as subcategories beneath it. Click any category. Omani intangible heritage Oral traditions Proverbs Folktales Traditional crafts Weaving Pottery Performing arts Traditional music Traditional dance

entries.heading: A taxonomy for the Dhofar University academic guide
entries.text: Suppose we design an academic guide that helps Dhofar University students find their degree programs and courses. We start with the university and move from the most general level to the most specific. The example follows the undergraduate catalogue for 2024–2025, College of Arts and Applied Sciences. University Dhofar University College College of Arts and Applied Sciences Department Department of Computer Science Degree program Bachelor of Science in Computer Science Course Programming Fundamentals (COMP 111) Course Discrete Structures (COMP 151) Course Data Structures and Algorithms (COMP 201)

entries.heading: Tag a source, narrow the search
entries.text: When you add a recorded proverb to your RAG system, you can tag it as Oral traditions → Proverbs. Then, if a student asks for Omani proverbs, the system can use that tag to narrow its search to the relevant sources. Pick a category in the heritage tree above and watch the search space shrink. A student asks: “Tell me some Omani proverbs” Searching 2 of 8 sources · Oral traditions → Proverbs A proverb recorded in an interview with an elder Proverbs A page from a printed collection of proverbs Proverbs A folktale told by a grandmother Folktales The transcript of a folktale Folktales A video of a weaving demonstration Weaving Notes from a pottery workshop Pottery A recording of traditional music Traditional music A video of a traditional dance performance Traditional dance

entries.heading: What a taxonomy looks like: a tree of categories
entries.text: Start with a broad category at the top, then follow its branches to more specific categories. Here is an example for the Dhofar University academic guide. The middle boxes are categories you could create for the guide; the bottom boxes are individual courses listed under those categories. Computer Science Courses Programming Courses COMP 111 · Programming Fundamentals Mathematics Courses COMP 151 · Discrete Structures Data Structures and Algorithms Courses COMP 201 · Data Structures and Algorithms Click a course at the bottom to see the branches a student follows to reach it. Add a new programming course Read each branch as “belongs under this category”. To find COMP 111, a student follows Computer Science Courses → Programming Courses → Programming Fundamentals. If you add a new programming course, the same tree shows where to put it.

entries.heading: What is an ontology?
entries.text: A taxonomy organises information into categories and subcategories, making it easier to find and classify. An ontology can include that hierarchy and also describe the entities involved, their attributes, and how they relate to one another. It can also define rules or constraints that a system uses to draw conclusions or check information.

entries.heading: From taxonomy to ontology at Dhofar University
entries.text: Dhofar University College of Arts and Applied Sciences Department of Computer Science BSc in Computer Science COMP 111 · COMP 151 · COMP 201 In the Dhofar University example, the hierarchy helps a student find a course in the study plan. The ontology can specify that a course has a credit value (an attribute), that one course requires another (a relationship), and that passing the required course satisfies that prerequisite (a rule). Put simply: the taxonomy helps a student find the course. The ontology helps the system explain how that course fits into the student’s program and what the student needs in order to take it.

entries.heading: A practical approach: start with a taxonomy, then build an ontology around it
entries.text: Organise the information. Start with the hierarchy University → College → Department → Degree program → Courses. This helps students find where a course appears in the guide. Describe what the connections mean. A department offers a degree program. A student enrols in a program. COMP 201 requires COMP 151. The ontology can also describe attributes, such as a course’s credit hours, and rules, such as “passing COMP 151 satisfies that prerequisite for COMP 201”.

entries.heading: The four building blocks of an ontology
entries.text: Concept Example from the Dhofar University guide Group COMP 151 and COMP 201 both belong to the category Course. Property A course has a code, a title and a credit value. Relationship COMP 201 requires COMP 151. Rule If a student passes COMP 151, they satisfy that prerequisite for COMP 201. A taxonomy tells us which group something belongs to. An ontology describes what properties it has, how it connects to other things, and what we can infer from those connections when rules are defined.

entries.heading: How does an ontology look?
entries.text: An ontology often looks like a map of boxes connected by labelled arrows. Each arrow tells you exactly what the connection means. For example, the arrow from a student to a degree program says “is enrolled in”, while the arrow between two courses says “requires”.

entries.heading: The definitions: types and the arrows allowed between them
entries.text: enrolls in includes has passed requires Student Degree Program Course Read each arrow as a sentence (click one): A student enrols in a degree program. A degree program includes courses. A student can pass a course. The loop on Course means that one course can require another course.

entries.heading: The definitions in use: example records
entries.text: is enrolled in includes requires has passed Student: Maryam Program: Computer Science Course: COMP 201 Course: COMP 151 Read each arrow as a sentence (click one): Maryam is enrolled in the Computer Science program. The program includes COMP 201. COMP 201 requires COMP 151. Maryam has passed COMP 151. The ontology defines the vocabulary and its meaning. It defines types such as Student, Degree Program and Course. It can specify that a course has properties such as a course code and credit hours, and that “requires” connects one course to another. The second diagram shows those definitions used with example records like Maryam and COMP 201.

entries.heading: Add a rule, and the system can reach a conclusion
entries.text: Rule: if a student has passed a course that another course requires, the student has satisfied that prerequisite. The archive records that Maryam has passed COMP 151 Apply the rule

entries.heading: Spot the difference: a tree of categories or a map of connections
Taxonomy
entries.text: A tree. You follow branches from broader groups down to narrower groups, and every branch means the same thing: “belongs under”.

entries.heading: Ontology
entries.text: A map. You can follow several kinds of connections, and the label on each arrow tells you what it means: enrols in, includes, requires, has passed. A taxonomy organises information into categories and subcategories. An ontology defines how things are related and can include rules for drawing conclusions from those relationships.

entries.heading: What is RDF?
entries.text: RDF (Resource Description Framework) is a standard for describing information in a structured, connected and machine-readable way. Instead of ordinary paragraphs, RDF breaks information into small statements, each made of three parts. These statements are called RDF triples.

entries.heading: 1 · Why three parts?
entries.text: Subject What are we describing? Predicate What are we saying about it? Object What entity or value is associated with it? Mirbat located within Dhofar One triple is one complete statement: Mirbat is located within Dhofar. These three components are enough to describe a very large variety of information.

entries.heading: 2 · Converting ordinary information into RDF
entries.text: Imagine we collected this paragraph during Omani intangible heritage research (an illustrative example). A person understands it at once; RDF makes each fact and relationship explicit for a computer. Click a triple to see which words it comes from. Ahmed , a 78-year-old narrator , narrated a version of a traditional folktale called The Wise Fisherman . The story was recorded in Mirbat , which is located in Dhofar , Oman . Subject Predicate Object Ahmed is a Narrator Ahmed has age 78 Version 001 narrated by Ahmed Version 001 is version of The Wise Fisherman Version 001 recorded in Mirbat Mirbat located within Dhofar Dhofar located within Oman Extract them one at a time 7 of 7 statements We have transformed one paragraph into seven structured statements.

entries.heading: 3 · Why describing information in a connected way matters
entries.text: This is where the real power of RDF appears: the object of one triple can become the subject of another. Each triple connects to others through shared entities. Version 001 recorded in Mirbat Mirbat located within Dhofar Dhofar located within Oman Mirbat is the object of the first triple but the subject of the second. Dhofar is the object of the second but the subject of the third. This is how individual statements grow into a network of connected knowledge.

entries.heading: 4 · Why not simply use ordinary text?
entries.text: Ordinary text RDF Information is written in paragraphs. Information is represented as individual statements. Relationships may be implicit. Relationships are explicit. Entities may be ambiguous. Entities can have unique identifiers. Connections must be extracted. Connections are directly represented. Reasoning requires interpretation. Formal reasoning is possible with appropriate ontology rules. Primarily designed for human reading. Designed for machine-readable knowledge representation. RDF does not necessarily replace the original text. It provides a structured representation of the knowledge contained within that text.

entries.heading: 5 · How many triples form a knowledge graph
entries.text: Draw every triple as an arrow and the seven statements become one connected picture. Click a box to see every triple it takes part in. Now imagine doing this for thousands of stories, narrators, places, traditions and historical documents: you could search for connections across the whole collection, rather than searching each document on its own. is a has age narrated by is version of recorded in located within located within Narrator Ahmed 78 The Wise Fisherman Version 001 Mirbat Oman Dhofar Click a box: Mirbat and Dhofar are both subject and object.

entries.heading: 6 · Where does the ontology fit into RDF?
entries.text: RDF provides the mechanism for describing connected information. The ontology provides the formal meaning and logic behind those descriptions. Both are written as RDF triples and can be stored in the same Turtle file.

entries.heading: An RDF statement describes a fact
entries.text: :Mirbat :locatedWithin :Dhofar .

entries.heading: An ontology definition gives the relationship its logic
entries.text: :locatedWithin a owl:TransitiveProperty . Transitive means: if A is within B, and B is within C, then A is within C.

entries.heading: The whole example as one Turtle file (.ttl)
entries.text: @prefix : <http://example.org/heritage#> . @prefix owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> . # Ontology: the meaning and logic of a relationship :locatedWithin a owl:TransitiveProperty . # Facts from the interview (one triple per statement) :Ahmed a :Narrator ; :hasAge 78 . :Version001 :narratedBy :Ahmed ; :isVersionOf :TheWiseFisherman ; :recordedIn :Mirbat . :Mirbat :locatedWithin :Dhofar . :Dhofar :locatedWithin :Oman . Ask: Is Mirbat located within Oman? No triple says so directly. Run the reasoning engine

entries.heading: 7 · The complete picture
entries.text: Raw data The original information we collected. Taxonomy Classifies information into categories. Ontology Defines concepts, meanings, relationships and logic. RDF Represents definitions and facts as connected triples. Knowledge graph The resulting network of connected knowledge. Reasoning engine Derives additional facts using the available knowledge and logical rules.

entries.heading: 8 · The most important idea to remember
entries.text: Think of RDF triples as LEGO building blocks. Each block is a small piece of knowledge, and because the blocks connect, we can build an enormous structure of knowledge. RDF provides the building blocks. Ontology defines the meaning of the blocks and the logic of their connections. Knowledge graph is the structure created by connecting those blocks. Reasoning engine discovers what logically follows from those connections. The importance of RDF is not simply that it describes information, but that it describes it in a way that lets individual facts be connected, searched, shared and logically interpreted by computers.

entries.heading: RDF files and Turtle: from facts to a diagram
entries.text: An RDF file stores facts in a way that lets a computer connect them and follow those connections. RDF stands for Resource Description Framework. The file is plain text; a visualizer can turn the same text into a diagram of boxes and arrows.

entries.heading: 1 · In RDF, information is stored as a set of triples
entries.text: Part What it means Heritage example Subject The thing you’re describing Recording 15 Predicate The relationship or property you’re describing was recorded in Object The thing it links to, or the value of the property Mirbat So “Recording 15 was recorded in Mirbat” is one triple. Each triple expresses one statement with three parts: subject → predicate → object. Recording 15 → has a duration of → 12 minutes is another. Together, these triples describe the same recording.

entries.heading: Why three parts?
entries.text: RDF uses triples because three parts are enough to express one link. You need to know: What you’re describing. How it’s connected. What it’s connected to. Recording 15 was recorded in Mirbat Remove the predicate The predicate tells you exactly what the link means: the recording was made in Mirbat.

entries.heading: 2 · Why triples, when a table can store the same information?
entries.text: Both structures work, but they organise the meaning differently. Both can tell you that Recording 15 was recorded in Mirbat. The difference is where you look to understand what “Mirbat” means.

entries.heading: In a table, look at the column heading
entries.text: Recording Recorded in Discusses Recording 15 Mirbat Salalah How do you know that Mirbat is where the recording was made and Salalah is what it talks about? You read the column headings: each heading tells you how to interpret the value below it.

entries.heading: In RDF, look at the predicate in each statement
entries.text: Subject Predicate Object Recording 15 was recorded in Mirbat Recording 15 discusses Salalah Here each triple names the relationship directly. If someone shares just one triple with you, you can still tell what it means. Share the values without the headings, and one triple on its own

entries.heading: 3 · What is an identifier?
entries.text: An identifier is a unique reference your application uses for one specific thing. In the heritage graph, h:Mirbat is the short form of the example identifier https://example.org/heritage/Mirbat. turtle h:Recording15 h:wasRecordedIn h:Mirbat . h:Mirbat h:hasName "Mirbat" . h:Mirbat h:hasName "مرباط" . Show the full identifiers In the file What it means h:Mirbat The identifier for the town "Mirbat" The town’s name in English "مرباط" The town’s name in Arabic One town can have several names. Because all three statements use the same identifier, your application knows that the recording location and both names refer to the same town.

entries.heading: Namespace and prefix
entries.text: h: is the shortcut for https://example.org/heritage/. That shared part is called a namespace. You add a name after h: to get the identifier for a specific thing. So h: is the prefix, and h:Mirbat is the short form of the identifier for Mirbat. Short form in Turtle Full identifier h:Mirbat <https://example.org/heritage/Mirbat> h:Recording15 <https://example.org/heritage/Recording15>

entries.heading: 4 · What is a Turtle file?
entries.text: A Turtle file is a plain-text file that writes RDF triples in a compact, readable form. Its usual file extension is .ttl, as in heritage.ttl. Why is it called Turtle? The name stands for Terse RDF Triple Language. Terse means brief or compact: for example, Turtle lets you define h: once and reuse it as a shortcut for a long identifier. heritage.ttl @prefix h: <https://example.org/heritage/> . h:Recording15 h:wasRecordedIn h:Mirbat . h:Mirbat h:isLocatedIn h:Dhofar . Click a line of the file to see what it does. subject predicate object prefix Subject Predicate Object What it says h:Recording15 h:wasRecordedIn h:Mirbat Recording 15 was recorded in Mirbat. h:Mirbat h:isLocatedIn h:Dhofar Mirbat is located in Dhofar. Notice how h:Mirbat appears at the end of the first triple and at the start of the second. The shared identifier is what connects the two facts into a path: Recording 15 → Mirbat → Dhofar. RDF describes each fact as a subject, predicate and object; Turtle is the set of writing rules used to put those triples into the text file. The lines can appear in any order and still describe the same graph.

entries.heading: 5 · RDF, knowledge graph and diagram
entries.text: RDF — how we express the facts. The RDF file stores the knowledge graph as text (here, heritage.ttl). People can read the triples directly, and software can query the relationships they describe. Knowledge graph — the network those facts form: the set of connected facts, such as Recording 15 being recorded in Mirbat and Mirbat being located in Dhofar. Diagram — a picture of that network. A visualizer draws the same relationships as nodes and arrows, so people can see the connections at a glance. Same facts. One connected network. A picture people can read.

entries.heading: 6 · Try it: a Turtle visualizer
entries.text: RDF records how individual items are classified and connected, in a form a computer can read. A visualization tool then draws them as boxes and arrows. Pick an example file or type your own lines: the diagram redraws as you type. Try adding h:Recording27 h:wasRecordedIn h:Mirbat . or shuffling the lines. heritage.ttl: two facts Two recordings, one town One town, two names Everything about Recording 15 Two files, two prefixes The RDF file (Turtle text). Edit it. @prefix h: <https://example.org/heritage/> . h:Recording15 h:wasRecordedIn h:Mirbat . h:Mirbat h:isLocatedIn h:Dhofar . h:Recording27 h:wasRecordedIn h:Mirbat . Shuffle the lines 3 triples → 4 boxes, 3 arrows What a visualizer draws was recorded in is located in was recorded in Recording 15 Mirbat Dhofar Recording 27 Subject Predicate Object Line Recording 15 was recorded in Mirbat 2 Mirbat is located in Dhofar 3 Recording 27 was recorded in Mirbat 4 Each row becomes one labelled arrow. The file names things 6 times, but the diagram has only 4 boxes: Mirbat (3×) is drawn once, because every mention uses the same identifier. Click a box to see its arrows.

entries.heading: 7 · Shared identifiers turn facts into paths
entries.text: When every triple uses the same identifier for Mirbat, the triples share one Mirbat node. It can be the subject in one triple and the object in another, and a question can walk from fact to fact. turtle @prefix h: <https://example.org/heritage/> . h:Recording15 h:wasRecordedIn h:Mirbat . h:Mirbat h:isLocatedIn h:Dhofar . h:Recording27 h:wasRecordedIn h:Mirbat . Triple Where h:Mirbat appears What the triple says 1 Object Recording 15 was recorded in Mirbat. 2 Subject Mirbat is located in Dhofar. 3 Object Recording 27 was recorded in Mirbat. was recorded in is located in was recorded in Recording 15 Mirbat Dhofar Recording 27 Ask: which of these recordings were made in Dhofar? This works across files too, once the application reads both files. It matches the full identifier https://example.org/heritage/Mirbat, so another file could use a different prefix, such as heritage:Mirbat, and still refer to the same node. Try “Two files, two prefixes” in the visualizer above.

entries.heading: 8 · From raw information to linked knowledge
entries.text: Gather Raw information: an interview, a recording, a note. Break into triples One statement each: subject → predicate → object. Give identifiers One identifier for one thing, so every mention means the same thing. Write the Turtle file The triples saved as text in heritage.ttl. Knowledge graph Shared identifiers join the facts into one network. Draw, search, use A diagram people can read, questions that follow links, clear facts for AI. Why it matters: once facts are linked, search can follow connections across a whole collection instead of matching words in one document at a time, and AI systems get facts whose meaning is explicit, with a source for each one, for answering questions (as in RAG) and for preparing training data.

entries.heading: What is a knowledge graph?
entries.text: A knowledge graph is a network-based representation of knowledge in which entities are connected by typed relationships. It answers: how are concepts connected in a machine-readable network? The ontology is the plan: the types and the arrows allowed between them. The knowledge graph is the data that follows the plan: real entities such as Maryam, COMP 151 or the Omani khanjar, and one arrow for every fact. Each fact is stored as a triple: subject, relation, object, which is exactly what RDF writes down (see the RDF triples part).

entries.heading: The Dhofar University facts as triples
entries.text: (Maryam, is_enrolled_in, ComputerScience) (ComputerScience, includes, COMP201) (COMP201, requires, COMP151) (Maryam, has_passed, COMP151)

entries.heading: A heritage knowledge graph: ask it a question
entries.text: What is the khanjar made of? When is it worn? Which source says so? made_of made_of made_of worn_at worn_at part_of documented_in Al-Khanjar Silver Leather Wood Weddings National events Men’s traditional dress UNESCO record, 2022 ( khanjar , made_of , silver ) ( khanjar , made_of , leather ) ( khanjar , made_of , wood ) ( khanjar , worn_at , weddings ) ( khanjar , worn_at , national ) ( khanjar , part_of , dress ) ( khanjar , documented_in , unesco ) Each fact is a triple: subject, relation, object. Because the links are typed, a question becomes a walk along one kind of link, and every answer can point back to its source. These facts come from the UNESCO record on Al-Khanjar.

entries.heading: What is semantics?
entries.text: Semantics is the meaning of concepts, terms and relationships. It answers: what does this information mean? Without it, two systems can use the same word for different things, or different words for the same thing.

entries.heading: Many words, one meaning
entries.text: الخنجر Al-Khanjar khanjar Omani dagger heritage:Khanjar Four labels point to one concept ID, so a search for any of them finds the same element and its facts.

entries.heading: One word, two meanings
entries.text: silver a material: the khanjar is made of it material:Silver silver a colour: a grey, shiny shade colour:Silver Without a definition, “made of silver” and “silver-coloured” look the same to a computer. A clear concept ID removes the doubt.

entries.heading: Links have meaning too
entries.text: worn_at Defined as “an occasion at which the object is customarily worn”. It does not mean where it was made or sold. Defining the link keeps every system that reads it in agreement.

entries.heading: One course, several names
entries.text: COMP 201 Data Structures and Algorithms هياكل البيانات والخوارزميات The code, the English title and the Arabic title must point to the same course, or a student searching in Arabic will miss it.

entries.heading: What does “requires” mean?
entries.text: requires Defined as “must be passed before a student can register”, not “is recommended before”. The rule about prerequisites only works because this meaning is fixed.

entries.heading: Putting it together
entries.text: Taxonomy, ontology, knowledge graph and semantics are not competitors. Each adds one layer: structure, then meaning and rules, then connected facts, then shared understanding.

entries.heading: At a glance: focus, strength and limitation
entries.text: Idea Focus Main strength Main limitation Taxonomy Classification and parent–child structure Simple to organise and easy to navigate Usually cannot express relationships beyond the hierarchy Ontology Meaning, rules and relationships Far more expressive than a taxonomy More complex to design and maintain Knowledge graph Connected data and entity relationships Flexible, scalable, and useful for querying and inference Only as useful as the schema, ontology or data behind it Semantics Interpretation and meaning Consistent understanding across systems and contexts Meaning can vary unless it is clearly defined

entries.heading: How they relate: from classification to meaning
entries.text: Taxonomy provides the hierarchical structure . Ontology adds formal meaning and richer relationship modelling . Knowledge graph represents those concepts as linked entities and relations . Semantics gives the concepts and links their meaning, so they are interpreted correctly . The key difference in one line each: taxonomy is about classification, ontology about defining concepts and their relations, a knowledge graph about representing and connecting knowledge, and semantics about meaning and interpretation.

entries.heading: In AI and RAG
entries.text: The region, dialect and source-type labels on a TurathAI record are a small taxonomy, and they power the filters in the vector database. A knowledge graph can sit beside the vectors: vector search finds passages that sound relevant, and the graph answers exact relationship questions and links each fact to its source. Combining the two is often called GraphRAG.

entries.heading: In neuroscience
entries.text: Brain atlases arrange regions in a hierarchy, a taxonomy of the brain. Neuroscience ontologies define cell types, their properties and how they connect, so that labs can share data. And semantic memory, our store of facts and the meanings of concepts, is often described as a network of linked concepts, much like a knowledge graph. Summary. Taxonomy organises concepts, ontology defines their meaning and relationships, a knowledge graph connects them into a usable structure, and semantics ensures the system understands what the concepts and links mean. Together they move from simple classification to rich, machine-readable knowledge.

entries.heading: Classroom glossary
entries.text: Every word used in the labs, in plain language. A neuron combines its weighted inputs and its bias, then applies an activation rule; everything else builds on that. 45 terms

entries.heading: Neuron
entries.text: A small calculator. It multiplies each input by a weight, adds the results, adds a bias, and passes the total through an activation rule. output = activation(2 × 0.5 + 3 × 1 + (−1)) = activation(3) See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Input
entries.text: A number that enters the network, or a value that arrives from the previous layer. The area of a house, a pixel’s brightness, or another neuron’s output. See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Weight
entries.text: The strength and direction of one connection. A large weight makes its input matter more; a negative weight makes the input push the total down. Input 3 with weight 0.5 contributes 1.5. With weight −0.5 it contributes −1.5. See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Weighted sum
entries.text: Every input multiplied by its weight, then all of those products added together. Written Σ (sigma). 2 × 0.5 + 3 × 1 = 1 + 3 = 4 See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Bias
entries.text: One extra number the neuron adds after the weighted sum. It shifts the total up or down, which decides how easily the neuron switches on. Sum 4 with bias −1 gives z = 3. With bias −5 it gives z = −1. See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Pre-activation (z)
entries.text: The neuron’s total before the activation: weighted sum + bias. z = 4 + (−1) = 3 See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Activation function
entries.text: The rule that turns z into the neuron’s output. Without a non-linear activation, many layers would collapse into one straight-line calculation. ReLU(−3) = 0, ReLU(3) = 3. Sigmoid(0) = 0.5. See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: ReLU
entries.text: The most common activation: negative totals become 0, positive totals pass through unchanged. max(0, z) See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Sigmoid
entries.text: An activation that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, useful as a “how strongly yes” score. sigmoid(−0.2) ≈ 0.45 See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Output (a)
entries.text: The value a neuron passes on. The outputs of the last layer are the network’s prediction. See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Layer
entries.text: A group of neurons that all read the same inputs and work side by side. See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Hidden layer
entries.text: A layer between the inputs and the outputs. Its neurons learn intermediate features that the next layer combines. See it in Playground

entries.heading: Forward pass
entries.text: Calculating the output from the inputs, one layer after another, using the current weights and biases. See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Parameter
entries.text: Any number the network learns: every weight and every bias. “A model with 7 billion parameters” has 7 billion of these numbers. A 2 → 3 → 1 network has 2×3 + 3×1 = 9 weights and 3 + 1 = 4 biases: 13 parameters. See it in Advisor

entries.heading: Initialization
entries.text: Choosing the starting weights, usually small random numbers. The seed makes the same “random” numbers appear every time. See it in Explore the network

entries.heading: Deep learning
entries.text: Machine learning with networks that have many layers, so that each layer can build on the features found by the one before.

entries.heading: Target
entries.text: The correct answer for one example: what we want the network to output. See it in Teach the network

entries.heading: Loss
entries.text: One number that measures how wrong the predictions are. Training tries to make it as small as possible. Mean squared error: prediction 3, target 1 → (3 − 1)² = 4. See it in Teach the network

entries.heading: Gradient
entries.text: For one weight: how much the loss would change if that weight grew a little. Its sign says which way to move; its size says how much it matters. Gradient +2 means “raising this weight raises the loss”, so training lowers it. See it in Worked examples

entries.heading: Backpropagation
entries.text: The method that finds every gradient. It starts at the loss and works backward, layer by layer, multiplying the slopes along the way. See it in Worked examples

entries.heading: Chain rule
entries.text: If A changes B and B changes C, the effect of A on C is the two slopes multiplied. Backpropagation is this rule applied again and again. ∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂a × ∂a/∂z × ∂z/∂w See it in Worked examples

entries.heading: Delta (δ)
entries.text: A neuron’s share of the error: the error arriving at its output × the slope of its activation. δ = ∂L/∂a × f′(z) See it in Worked examples

entries.heading: Gradient descent
entries.text: The update rule: move every parameter a small step against its gradient. new weight = old weight − learning rate × gradient See it in Teach the network

entries.heading: Learning rate
entries.text: How big each update step is. Too large and the loss jumps around or grows; too small and learning is very slow. See it in Teach the network

entries.heading: Epoch
entries.text: One full pass over all the training examples. See it in House case

entries.heading: Batch
entries.text: A small group of examples used for one update. 1,000 examples in batches of 100 give 10 updates per epoch. See it in House case

entries.heading: Overfitting
entries.text: When a network memorises its training examples instead of learning the rule. Training loss keeps falling while test loss rises. See it in Playground

entries.heading: Training, validation, and test sets
entries.text: Three separate parts of the data: train to learn, validation to tune choices, test to judge once at the end. See it in House case

entries.heading: Dead ReLU
entries.text: A ReLU neuron whose total is always negative. Its output and its slope are both 0, so no error reaches it and it stops learning. See it in Worked examples

entries.heading: Regularization
entries.text: A small penalty on large weights that pushes the network toward simpler rules and reduces overfitting. See it in Playground

entries.heading: Large language model (LLM)
entries.text: A very large neural network trained to predict the next token of text. Everything it writes is produced one token at a time. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Token
entries.text: A piece of text the model works with: a word, part of a word, or punctuation. Each token has a number (its id). See it in Tokenizer

entries.heading: Vocabulary
entries.text: The full list of tokens a model knows. The model’s output is one probability for every entry. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Embedding
entries.text: A list of numbers that stands for a token. The numbers are learned, so tokens used in similar ways end up with similar vectors. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Position
entries.text: Extra numbers added to each embedding so the model knows where in the sentence a token sits. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Attention
entries.text: How a token gathers information from earlier tokens. It scores each earlier token, turns the scores into weights that add to 1, and takes a weighted sum of their values. In “the cat ran to the”, the last “the” reads mostly from “to” and “cat”. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Query, key, and value
entries.text: Three vectors made from each token. The query asks “what am I looking for?”, a key answers “what do I offer?”, and the value is what gets passed on. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Transformer
entries.text: The network design behind modern LLMs: attention to mix information between tokens, followed by an MLP, repeated in many layers. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: MLP
entries.text: A small stack of ordinary neuron layers. Inside a transformer it processes each token’s vector after attention. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Logit
entries.text: The raw score the model gives each possible next token, before it is turned into a probability. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Softmax
entries.text: The rule that turns a list of scores into probabilities that are all positive and add up to 1. Scores 2, 1, 0 → probabilities 0.67, 0.24, 0.09. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Cross-entropy
entries.text: The loss for next-token prediction: −log(probability the model gave the correct token). Confident and right is near 0; confident and wrong is large. Correct token given 90% → 0.105. Given 1% → 4.6. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Temperature
entries.text: A setting that sharpens or flattens the probabilities before a token is picked. Low is careful and repetitive; high is surprising. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Context window
entries.text: The number of most recent tokens the model can see at once. See it in LLM playground

entries.heading: Autoregressive
entries.text: Writing one token, adding it to the input, and predicting again. This loop is how an LLM produces whole sentences. See it in LLM playground
